question: Why is the hospital ward often described as an ecosystem during patient care?

question: Which physical factor in the ward helps to regulate a patient's natural circadian rhythm?

question: How does too much noise in a hospital ward affect a patient?

question: Where should used injection needles and blades be thrown away immediately after use?

question: A nurse finishes dressing a wound soaked with blood and pus. Where should this soiled dressing go?

options.D: In the infectious waste bin

question: What is the main reason for having a reliable running water supply in a health facility?

question: Why is poor food handling especially dangerous for new mothers in the maternity ward?

question: Which task best describes a nurse acting as an environmental manager in the ward?

question: What is an effective way for a nurse to involve patient relatives in keeping the ward clean?

question: What is the main reason a midwife performs a head-to-toe physical exam on an expectant mother?

question: Why is it helpful to follow a steady head-to-toe order during a physical assessment?

question: At what point during a clinic visit does the general survey begin?

options.C: Only after checking the patient's blood pressure and pulse
options.D: When the patient is lying completely flat on the examination couch

explanation: The general survey starts instantly upon visual contact, as you notice posture, breathing, and general distress without touching them. [learn more](BMP110_U6_T1#BMP110_U6_T1_h2)

question: A pregnant woman walks into the clinic looking pale, sweating, and holding her lower abdomen. Which part of the physical exam does this observation fall under?

options.A: Neurological reflex testing
options.B: Ophthalmic fundoscopy
options.C: Auscultation of breath sounds
options.D: The general survey

explanation: Initial visual observations of distress, pallor, and posture form the core of the general survey. [learn more](BMP110_U6_T1#BMP110_U6_T1_h2)

question: Which examination technique involves tapping the body surface with the fingers to check underlying tissues?

options.A: Inspection
options.B: Percussion
options.C: Auscultation
options.D: Palpation

explanation: Percussion uses tapping fingers to create sound waves that reveal whether underlying structures are solid, fluid, or full of air. [learn more](BMP110_U6_T1#BMP110_U6_T1_h3)

question: Why do midwives usually inspect a patient before doing palpation and percussion?

options.A: It replaces the need to document findings in the patient's case note
options.B: It is the only technique that requires the use of clinical equipment
options.C: It warms up the patient's skin so they do not feel cold during palpation
options.D: It allows you to observe normal appearance and spot abnormalities without altering them

explanation: Inspecting first gives you an unmanipulated view of the body before touch or pressure alters skin texture or pain responses. [learn more](BMP110_U6_T1#BMP110_U6_T1_h3)

question: What is a midwife looking for when pulling down a patient's lower eyelid to check the conjunctiva?

options.A: Bleeding caused by gum disease
options.B: Yellow discoloration indicating jaundice
options.C: Swelling caused by high blood pressure
options.D: Pallor indicating possible anemia

explanation: Pale conjunctiva is a classic physical sign of low hemoglobin levels or anemia during pregnancy. [learn more](BMP110_U6_T1#BMP110_U6_T1_h4)

question: Why might a pregnant woman's gums bleed easily during a routine check?

options.A: Hormonal changes during pregnancy cause increased gum sensitivity and vascularity
options.B: It indicates that the fetus is absorbing calcium from her teeth
options.C: It is always a sign of severe systemic leukemia in pregnancy
options.D: She is brushing her teeth too gently every morning

explanation: Pregnancy hormones increase blood flow to the gums, making them prone to swelling and mild bleeding known as pregnancy gingivitis. [learn more](BMP110_U6_T1#BMP110_U6_T1_h4)

question: What is the best way to get an accurate respiratory rate from a patient?

options.A: Place a heavy stethoscope directly over the patient's abdomen
options.B: Count breaths discreetly without telling the patient you are watching
options.C: Measure the exact speed of the radial pulse instead of breathing
options.D: Ask the patient to take deep breaths while you look at a wristwatch

explanation: Patients consciously or unconsciously change their breathing pattern if they know their respiration is being actively counted. [learn more](BMP110_U6_T1#BMP110_U6_T1_h5)

question: Why is a soft heart murmur frequently heard in normal, healthy pregnant women?

options.A: The heart muscle permanently shrinks during the first trimester
options.B: Increased blood volume and cardiac output create higher flow across normal valves
options.C: The growing uterus completely stops blood flow to the lower limbs
options.D: High levels of progesterone cause the heart valves to dissolve

explanation: The extra blood volume circulating during pregnancy increases flow speed, often producing a benign flow murmur. [learn more](BMP110_U6_T1#BMP110_U6_T1_h5)

question: Which abdominal examination step must always be done BEFORE you press on the belly?

options.A: Documentation
options.B: Percussion
options.C: Auscultation
options.D: Inspection

explanation: You listen with a stethoscope before pressing on the belly so you do not alter natural bowel sounds with your hands. [learn more](BMP110_U6_T1#BMP110_U6_T1_h6)

question: Why is deep palpation done after light palpation during an abdominal check?

options.A: To allow the stethoscope time to cool down against the skin
options.B: To check for fetal heart tones before feeling uterine contractions
options.C: To ensure bowel sounds are recorded before the stomach empties
options.D: To relax abdominal muscles and prevent startling the patient with sudden deep pressure

explanation: Starting with gentle touch relaxes the abdominal wall, making deeper touch more comfortable and accurate without muscle guarding. [learn more](BMP110_U6_T1#BMP110_U6_T1_h6)

question: Which reflex is routinely tested during antenatal checks to monitor for hypertensive disorders?

options.A: Triceps reflex
options.B: Achilles reflex
options.C: Biceps reflex
options.D: Patellar reflex

explanation: The knee-jerk or patellar reflex is the standard deep tendon reflex checked to monitor central nervous system irritability in pre-eclampsia. [learn more](BMP110_U6_T1#BMP110_U6_T1_h7)

question: What does pitting edema in the lower legs during late pregnancy usually mean?

options.A: Complete failure of the liver to produce red blood cells
options.B: Severe lack of calcium in the maternal diet
options.C: Excess fluid accumulation in the interstitial tissues
options.D: A permanent decrease in total maternal blood volume

explanation: Pitting edema occurs when fluid leaks out of blood vessels into surrounding tissues, leaving an indentation when pressed. [learn more](BMP110_U6_T1#BMP110_U6_T1_h7)

question: Which of these is a good example of objective clinical documentation?

options.A: Nothing unusual found anywhere on the body today
options.B: Skin pink, chest clear to auscultation bilaterally, patient alert
options.C: Normal checkup done without any problems at all
options.D: Patient looks completely okay and happy this morning

explanation: Objective documentation uses specific, measurable findings rather than vague personal opinions like 'okay' or 'fine'. [learn more](BMP110_U6_T1#BMP110_U6_T1_h8)

question: Why is it important to write down your findings right after a physical exam?

options.A: It provides an accurate legal record and ensures safe communication across shifts
options.B: It is required by law to be finished before the patient wakes up
options.C: It prevents the patient from asking questions about her test results
options.D: It replaces the verbal handover between incoming and outgoing midwives

explanation: Writing down findings right away prevents memory loss and gives every team member reliable facts for ongoing care. [learn more](BMP110_U6_T1#BMP110_U6_T1_h8)

question: What is the primary purpose of taking a patient's baseline vital signs?

options.A: To diagnose specific congenital infections
options.B: To confirm the exact gestational age of the fetus
options.C: To replace the need for routine physical examinations
options.D: To provide a comparative reference point for future changes

explanation: Baseline values give the midwife a standard measurement to compare against when monitoring a patient's progress or spotting sudden clinical deterioration. [learn more](BMP110_U6_T2#BMP110_U6_T2_h1)

question: Why should a midwife allow a client to rest before measuring her vital signs?

options.A: Patients refuse assessment if they are rushed into it
options.B: It gives the midwife time to complete all required paperwork
options.C: Resting lowers the body temperature to a baseline level
options.D: Physical exertion and anxiety can falsely alter the readings

explanation: Allowing brief rest helps eliminate temporary spikes in pulse and blood pressure caused by walking or stress. [learn more](BMP110_U6_T2#BMP110_U6_T2_h1)

question: What body temperature reading is generally classified as pyrexia or fever?

options.A: Above 38.0°C
options.B: Below 35.0°C
options.C: Exactly 37.0°C
options.D: Between 35.0°C and 36.0°C

explanation: A temperature reading exceeding 38.0°C indicates a fever, which requires further investigation for possible infection. [learn more](BMP110_U6_T2#BMP110_U6_T2_h2)

question: Why must a midwife ensure a patient's axilla is dry before taking her temperature?

options.A: Wet skin prevents the thermometer from staying in place
options.B: Moisture cools the skin surface and causes a falsely low reading
options.C: Sweat damages the electronic sensors inside the thermometer
options.D: Dry skin speeds up the transfer of heat to make the test faster

explanation: Evaporation of sweat cools the armpit, leading to an inaccurate measurement that does not reflect the true core body temperature. [learn more](BMP110_U6_T2#BMP110_U6_T2_h2)

question: Which artery is most commonly used for routine pulse assessment in an adult client?

options.A: Radial artery
options.B: Brachial artery
options.C: Carotid artery
options.D: Femoral artery

explanation: The radial artery located at the wrist is easily accessible and serves as the standard site for routine pulse checks. [learn more](BMP110_U6_T2#BMP110_U6_T2_h3)

question: What does a pulse rate above 100 beats per minute in a postpartum woman typically indicate?

options.A: Severe hypothermia and circulatory collapse
options.B: Bradycardia, which is normal after delivery
options.C: Normal resting cardiac output during recovery
options.D: Tachycardia, which may suggest bleeding or infection

explanation: A high heart rate after childbirth serves as an early warning sign for postpartum hemorrhage or developing sepsis. [learn more](BMP110_U6_T2#BMP110_U6_T2_h3)

question: What is the normal resting respiratory rate for a healthy adult?

options.A: 40 to 50 breaths per minute
options.B: 25 to 35 breaths per minute
options.C: 12 to 20 breaths per minute
options.D: 8 to 11 breaths per minute

explanation: A resting respiratory rate between 12 and 20 breaths per minute falls within normal physiological limits for adults. [learn more](BMP110_U6_T2#BMP110_U6_T2_h4)

question: Why is it best to count a patient's respirations without telling them you are doing it?

options.A: Patients often forget how to breathe if they focus on it
options.B: It saves time during a busy antenatal clinic shift
options.C: Unaware patients have a slower pulse rate as well
options.D: Conscious awareness can alter their natural breathing pattern

explanation: When people know their breathing is being watched, they tend to change their rate and depth unconsciously, yielding inaccurate data. [learn more](BMP110_U6_T2#BMP110_U6_T2_h4)

question: What does the first clear tapping sound heard through the stethoscope represent during blood pressure measurement?

options.A: Pulse pressure
options.B: Diastolic pressure
options.C: Mean arterial pressure
options.D: Systolic pressure

explanation: The onset of Korotkoff sounds, marked by the first tapping sound, corresponds to the systolic blood pressure. [learn more](BMP110_U6_T2#BMP110_U6_T2_h5)

question: Why is accurate blood pressure monitoring especially critical in antenatal care units?

options.A: It replaces the need to test urine for protein during visits
options.B: Pregnant women always have high blood pressure due to extra fluid
options.C: It is the only way to calculate the exact weight of the baby
options.D: It helps detect early signs of pre-eclampsia and hypertension

explanation: Routine blood pressure checks catch dangerous pregnancy-induced hypertensive disorders before they progress to eclamptic fits. [learn more](BMP110_U6_T2#BMP110_U6_T2_h5)

question: Where is the normal apex beat of the heart located in an adult?

options.A: Fourth intercostal space at the anterior axillary line
options.B: Fifth intercostal space at the midclavicular line
options.C: Sixth intercostal space near the xiphoid process
options.D: Second intercostal space at the sternal border

explanation: The normal point of maximal impulse is found in the left fifth intercostal space near the midclavicular line. [learn more](BMP110_U6_T2#BMP110_U6_T2_h6)

question: What does an apex beat that is displaced far to the left of the midclavicular line suggest?

options.A: A normal physiological variant
options.B: Enlargement of the heart
options.C: Low systemic blood pressure
options.D: Extreme dehydration in the client

explanation: Displacement of the apex beat away from its normal position often points to ventricular hypertrophy or cardiomegaly. [learn more](BMP110_U6_T2#BMP110_U6_T2_h6)

question: Which of the following is NOT required when documenting vital signs in a clinical chart?

options.A: The time the assessment was performed
options.B: The personal home address of the patient
options.C: The numerical values obtained
options.D: The exact date of the measurement

explanation: While patient identification is necessary on the folder, the home address is not a required component of a vital sign entry. [learn more](BMP110_U6_T2#BMP110_U6_T2_h7)

question: Why is plotting vital signs on a chart or partograph better than just writing numbers in text?

options.A: Written numbers are legally invalid in Nigerian hospitals
options.B: It removes the need for midwives to sign their names
options.C: Charts prevent patients from reading their own medical records
options.D: It makes it easier to visualize trends and spot sudden changes

explanation: Graphical representation allows clinicians to track progressive improvement or deterioration far quicker than scanning through rows of written digits. [learn more](BMP110_U6_T2#BMP110_U6_T2_h7)

question: What does anthropometry primarily measure?

options.A: Electrical activity within the central nervous system
options.B: Size, weight, and proportions of the human body
options.C: Chemical concentrations found in routine blood samples
options.D: Cellular responses during an active immune reaction

explanation: Anthropometry focuses entirely on the physical dimensions and structural proportions of the human body. [learn more](BMP110_U6_T3#BMP110_U6_T3_h1)

question: Why do midwives routinely collect anthropometric data from pregnant women?

options.A: To determine the exact gestational age using physical weight alone
options.B: To measure the precise hormonal output of the placenta
options.C: To diagnose exact chromosomal abnormalities in the developing fetus
options.D: To track nutritional status and identify potential pregnancy risks

explanation: Physical measurements help midwives spot nutritional deficits or excessive weight gain that could complicate pregnancy. [learn more](BMP110_U6_T3#BMP110_U6_T3_h1)

question: What is the first step a midwife should take with a weighing scale before a patient steps on it?

options.A: Wipe the foot platform thoroughly with a strong bleaching solution
options.B: Calibrate the internal springs using a standard one-kilogram weight
options.C: Balance and adjust the scale indicator to zero
options.D: Lock the mechanical wheels to prevent any movement on the floor

explanation: Checking that the scale rests at zero prevents baseline errors before a patient is weighed. [learn more](BMP110_U6_T3#BMP110_U6_T3_h2)

question: A pregnant woman steps up to the scale wearing a heavy wrapper and sandals. What action should the midwife take?

options.A: Record her weight immediately and subtract three kilograms for clothes
options.B: Ask her to remove her sandals and heavy outer garments
options.C: Add her estimated clothing weight directly into the clinical register
options.D: Refuse to record the weight until her next antenatal visit

explanation: Removing heavy clothing and shoes ensures the recorded weight reflects true body mass rather than extra items. [learn more](BMP110_U6_T3#BMP110_U6_T3_h2)

question: Which anatomical plane should be aligned when positioning a patient for an accurate height measurement?

options.A: Sagittal midline plane
options.B: Coronal facial plane
options.C: Transverse pelvic plane
options.D: Frankfort horizontal plane

explanation: Aligning the line of sight so that the ear canal and eye socket are level keeps the head in the correct upright position. [learn more](BMP110_U6_T3#BMP110_U6_T3_h3)

question: Why must the midwife lower the headpiece onto the crown of the patient's head during height measurement?

options.A: To lock the vertical sliding mechanism in place before reading the scale
options.B: To compress the hair and ensure the measurement touches the scalp
options.C: To test the mechanical strength of the sliding stadiometer rod
options.D: To encourage the patient to stand up straight and stretch taller

explanation: Thick hair can add false centimeters to a height reading if the headpiece is not pressed down securely. [learn more](BMP110_U6_T3#BMP110_U6_T3_h3)

question: On a traditional mechanical beam-balance scale, which weight sliding notch should be adjusted first?

options.A: The bottom calibration spring screw
options.B: Both weights at the exact same time
options.C: The smaller fine-tuning weight
options.D: The larger weight notch

explanation: Adjusting the larger weight first brings the beam close to balance before fine-tuning with the smaller weight. [learn more](BMP110_U6_T3#BMP110_U6_T3_h4)

question: Why is it important to use the same weighing scale for a woman across multiple antenatal visits?

options.A: To reduce calibration discrepancies between different instruments
options.B: To prevent the clinic from losing track of portable equipment
options.C: To comply with federal hospital equipment purchasing rules
options.D: To save time during busy morning antenatal clinic hours

explanation: Different scales can have slight calibration differences that make true weight change hard to track. [learn more](BMP110_U6_T3#BMP110_U6_T3_h4)

question: What is the primary clinical use of Mid-Upper Arm Circumference (MUAC) measurement in midwifery care?

options.A: Calculating precise fetal birth weight
options.B: Screening for acute malnutrition
options.C: Estimating maternal blood volume
options.D: Diagnosing gestational diabetes mellitus

explanation: MUAC provides a quick, reliable indicator of nutritional status and muscle wasting, especially in community settings. [learn more](BMP110_U6_T3#BMP110_U6_T3_h5)

question: Between which two anatomical landmarks is the tape placed when measuring Mid-Upper Arm Circumference?

options.A: Anterior superior iliac spine and the upper patella
options.B: First rib and the lower coastal margin of the thorax
options.C: Acromion process of the shoulder and olecranon process of the elbow
options.D: Clavicle notch and the midpoint of the sternum bone

explanation: The midpoint between the shoulder bone (acromion) and elbow bone (olecranon) is the standard site for MUAC. [learn more](BMP110_U6_T3#BMP110_U6_T3_h5)

question: What mathematical components are required to calculate a patient's Body Mass Index?

options.A: Weight in pounds multiplied by height in centimeters
options.B: Height in meters divided by weight in kilograms squared
options.C: Height in centimeters minus weight in kilograms
options.D: Weight in kilograms divided by height in meters squared

explanation: The standard BMI formula is weight in kg divided by the square of height in meters. [learn more](BMP110_U6_T3#BMP110_U6_T3_h6)

question: A non-pregnant woman has a calculated Body Mass Index of 28.5. How should a midwife classify this result?

options.A: Severely obese
options.B: Underweight
options.C: Normal weight
options.D: Overweight

explanation: A BMI reading between 25.0 and 29.9 falls into the overweight category. [learn more](BMP110_U6_T3#BMP110_U6_T3_h6)

question: Which metric units are standard for recording adult height and weight in clinical midwifery practice?

options.A: Millimeters for height and ounces for weight
options.B: Centimeters for height and kilograms for weight
options.C: Meters for height and grams for weight
options.D: Inches for height and pounds for weight

explanation: Standard medical documentation uses centimeters for height and kilograms for weight. [learn more](BMP110_U6_T3#BMP110_U6_T3_h7)

question: Why must a midwife document anthropometric measurements immediately after taking them rather than waiting?

options.A: To ensure the patient can check the math on her own calculator
options.B: To comply with hospital cafeteria break scheduling guidelines
options.C: To prevent transcription errors and loss of data from memory
options.D: To make the clinical pen run out of ink before the end of the day

explanation: Writing down numbers right away ensures accuracy and stops busy clinicians from mixing up patient figures. [learn more](BMP110_U6_T3#BMP110_U6_T3_h7)

question: What is the main reason for collecting a sputum sample?

options.A: To check the total red blood cell count
options.B: To measure the daily volume of fluid in the lungs
options.C: To identify germs causing lower respiratory infections
options.D: To measure blood oxygen levels in the lungs

explanation: Sputum examination helps healthcare providers find bacteria, fungi, or parasites causing infections deep in the lungs. [learn more](BMP110_U6_T4#BMP110_U6_T4_h1)

question: Why must the sample be true sputum instead of ordinary saliva?

options.A: Saliva contains digestive enzymes that destroy bacteria
options.B: Saliva changes color when exposed to room air
options.C: Saliva comes from the mouth and does not show what is happening in the lower airways
options.D: Saliva is too thick for glass slides

explanation: True sputum comes from the bronchi and lungs, while saliva only reflects the mouth. [learn more](BMP110_U6_T4#BMP110_U6_T4_h1)

question: When is the best time of day to collect a sputum sample?

options.A: Immediately after a heavy meal
options.B: Early in the morning immediately after waking up
options.C: Right after taking prescribed antibiotics
options.D: Late in the evening before sleeping

explanation: Secretions pool in the airways overnight, making the morning sample the most concentrated and productive for testing. [learn more](BMP110_U6_T4#BMP110_U6_T4_h2)

question: What should you tell a patient to use for mouth care before collecting a sputum sample?

options.A: Brush the teeth with medicated toothpaste
options.B: Clean the tongue using hydrogen peroxide
options.C: Use an antiseptic mouthwash
options.D: Rinse the mouth with plain water only

explanation: Plain water removes food particles and loose bacteria without leaving chemical residues that could ruin the lab culture. [learn more](BMP110_U6_T4#BMP110_U6_T4_h2)

question: What breathing technique helps a patient bring up secretions from deep in the chest?

options.A: Puckering the lips and blowing slowly
options.B: Taking slow, deep breaths followed by a strong cough
options.C: Taking quick, shallow breaths through the mouth
options.D: Holding the breath while lying flat

explanation: Deep breaths get air behind pooled secretions, and a forceful cough pushes the mucus up and out. [learn more](BMP110_U6_T4#BMP110_U6_T4_h3)

question: What should a midwife do if a patient is too weak to cough up sputum?

options.A: Collect ordinary saliva and label it as sputum
options.B: Wait several days until the patient regains strength
options.C: Scrape the back of the patient's throat with a cotton swab
options.D: Consult the medical officer for assistance like nebulized saline or physiotherapy

explanation: Weak patients often need clinical support like nebulization or physical therapy to help clear respiratory secretions. [learn more](BMP110_U6_T4#BMP110_U6_T4_h3)

question: What does thick, green, and pus-like sputum usually suggest?

options.A: Normal secretions from a healthy airway
options.B: Acute heart failure with fluid overload
options.C: An active bacterial infection in the respiratory tract
options.D: Early-stage viral bronchitis

explanation: Green or yellow sputum indicates white blood cells fighting off a bacterial infection in the lungs. [learn more](BMP110_U6_T4#BMP110_U6_T4_h4)

question: Which type of sputum is commonly seen in acute pulmonary oedema?

options.A: Pink and frothy
options.B: Dark brown and foul-smelling
options.C: Clear and watery
options.D: Thick and green

explanation: Fluid leaking into the air sacs mixes with air to create a pink, frothy sputum during acute heart failure. [learn more](BMP110_U6_T4#BMP110_U6_T4_h4)

question: Why is handling a sputum specimen considered high risk?

options.A: The mucus reacts with room air to produce toxic gas
options.B: The specimen container easily shatters
options.C: The sample can release infectious airborne droplets
options.D: The chemical preservatives cause skin burns

explanation: Coughing and handling respiratory secretions can spread germs like tuberculosis through the air if safety precautions are ignored. [learn more](BMP110_U6_T4#BMP110_U6_T4_h5)

question: What is the correct way to prepare a sputum container before sending it to the lab?

options.A: Leave the lid slightly loose so gases can escape
options.B: Place the open cup inside a paper envelope
options.C: Ensure the lid is tightly sealed and place the container inside a biohazard bag
options.D: Wipe the outside with soapy water and leave it on the tray

explanation: Sealing the container and using a biohazard bag prevents leaks and protects handlers from accidental exposure. [learn more](BMP110_U6_T4#BMP110_U6_T4_h5)

question: What happens if a sputum sample sits at room temperature for too long before reaching the lab?

options.A: All microorganisms die instantly from lack of oxygen
options.B: The sputum color turns permanently white
options.C: The mucus completely evaporates
options.D: Normal mouth bacteria overgrow and can mask the true infection

explanation: Leaving sputum at room temperature lets harmless mouth bacteria multiply quickly, which ruins test accuracy. [learn more](BMP110_U6_T4#BMP110_U6_T4_h6)

question: Which detail is NOT needed on a lab request form for a sputum test?

options.A: The patient's full name and hospital number
options.B: The patient's favorite recreational activities
options.C: The clinical diagnosis or reason for the test
options.D: The date and time of collection

explanation: Personal hobbies are not needed; the lab requires administrative and clinical details to process the test properly. [learn more](BMP110_U6_T4#BMP110_U6_T4_h6)

question: Why does a midwife check a patient's vomit?

options.A: To calculate amniotic fluid volume
options.B: To measure daily food calories
options.C: To check for internal bleeding or blockages
options.D: To confirm normal bowel bacteria

explanation: Checking vomit allows midwives to catch hidden complications like internal bleeding or blockages early. [learn more](BMP110_U6_T5#BMP110_U6_T5_h1)

question: Why is observing vomit part of a full physical check in midwifery?

options.A: It shows she is taking iron pills
options.B: It gives direct clues about upper digestive health
options.C: It tells the exact age of the pregnancy
options.D: It replaces checking blood pressure

explanation: Vomit acts as a physical sample of what is happening inside the upper gut when problems arise. [learn more](BMP110_U6_T5#BMP110_U6_T5_h1)

question: Which protective item is essential before collecting vomit?

options.A: Knee guards
options.B: A surgical cap
options.C: Non-sterile gloves
options.D: Heavy boots

explanation: Gloves create a barrier against infectious germs present in stomach fluids. [learn more](BMP110_U6_T5#BMP110_U6_T5_h2)

question: Why must a midwife explain the collection procedure to the patient first?

options.A: To reduce anxiety and gain her cooperation
options.B: To follow rules for minor surgery
options.C: To distract her from abdominal pain
options.D: To speed up food digestion

explanation: Clear communication helps a distressed patient feel secure and willing to assist during the process. [learn more](BMP110_U6_T5#BMP110_U6_T5_h2)

question: How should a vomiting patient be positioned to prevent choking?

options.A: Hanging upside down
options.B: Flat on her back with legs raised
options.C: Sitting up or turned to the side
options.D: Flat on her stomach

explanation: This safe position keeps fluid from flowing back down into the windpipe. [learn more](BMP110_U6_T5#BMP110_U6_T5_h3)

question: A woman vomits suddenly in bed. What should the midwife do first?

options.A: Write down the color in the notes
options.B: Turn her head to the side or help her sit up
options.C: Run to fetch a lab form
options.D: Throw away the basin of vomit

explanation: Clearing the airway and preventing choking is always the urgent first priority. [learn more](BMP110_U6_T5#BMP110_U6_T5_h3)

question: What does a coffee-ground look in vomit usually mean?

options.A: Old, partially digested blood
options.B: A reaction to prenatal vitamins
options.C: Fresh, active bleeding
options.D: High green vegetable intake

explanation: When blood sits in stomach acid for a while, it turns dark and grainy like coffee grounds. [learn more](BMP110_U6_T5#BMP110_U6_T5_h4)

question: What does a strong stool odor coming from vomit suggest?

options.A: High iron intake
options.B: Normal morning sickness
options.C: A mild stomach flu
options.D: An intestinal blockage

explanation: Fecal smelling vomit means contents from lower down the gut are backing up due to a blockage. [learn more](BMP110_U6_T5#BMP110_U6_T5_h4)

question: What does bright green or yellow vomit mean?

options.A: It contains bile from the small intestine
options.B: Fresh blood from the food pipe
options.C: Kidney failure
options.D: Normal digestion of breast milk

explanation: Bile naturally has a greenish-yellow color when pushed upward past the stomach valve. [learn more](BMP110_U6_T5#BMP110_U6_T5_h5)

question: Which finding in vomit must be reported immediately because it suggests missed medication or poisoning?

options.A: Clear watery liquid with foam
options.B: A pale yellow tint
options.C: Small amounts of saliva
options.D: Undigested pills

explanation: Finding whole pills means the body did not absorb them, raising concerns about treatment failure or toxic ingestion. [learn more](BMP110_U6_T5#BMP110_U6_T5_h5)

question: What specific detail must be included when writing down vomit notes?

options.A: The brand of the kidney bowl
options.B: Estimated volume in milliliters
options.C: The patient's favourite food
options.D: The name of the cleaning soap

explanation: Measuring volume helps track fluid loss and prevent dangerous dehydration. [learn more](BMP110_U6_T5#BMP110_U6_T5_h6)

question: A midwife records a patient's vomit. Which entry is the most professional?

options.A: 150ml of dark brown coffee-ground vomit with sour odor
options.B: Vomit collected with no strange objects
options.C: Patient threw up a lot of bad-looking stuff
options.D: A dirty basin of green fluid was emptied

explanation: Specific measurements, colors, and textures provide clear professional data for other health workers. [learn more](BMP110_U6_T5#BMP110_U6_T5_h6)

question: Where should liquid vomit be safely emptied?

options.A: Inside the handwashing sink
options.B: Into the clinical sluice hopper
options.C: Into an office dustbin
options.D: Out the hospital window

explanation: Sluice hoppers are designed for safe disposal of body fluids without contaminating handwashing sinks. [learn more](BMP110_U6_T5#BMP110_U6_T5_h7)

question: What is the final crucial step after disposing of vomit and cleaning equipment?

options.A: Write a research paper
options.B: Wash hands thoroughly with soap and water
options.C: Disinfect bedside curtains
options.D: Take a tea break

explanation: Hand hygiene stops the spread of infectious germs picked up during waste disposal. [learn more](BMP110_U6_T5#BMP110_U6_T5_h7)

question: During an antenatal visit, what does testing for protein in a pregnant woman's urine mainly help midwives screen for?

options.A: Iron deficiency anemia
options.B: Urinary tract infection
options.C: Gestational diabetes
options.D: Pre-eclampsia

explanation: Protein in the urine during pregnancy is a key sign of pre-eclampsia, which is why regular urine checks are important for keeping mothers safe. [learn more](BMP110_U6_T6#BMP110_U6_T6_h1)

question: Why is checking urine a standard and helpful tool in primary health care settings?

options.A: It provides a final diagnosis for all internal diseases
options.B: It replaces the need for any blood tests completely
options.C: It offers quick clues about kidney function and overall health
options.D: It is the only required diagnostic test during labor

explanation: Urine analysis gives fast, simple feedback on how well the kidneys and body are functioning without needing complex procedures. [learn more](BMP110_U6_T6#BMP110_U6_T6_h1)

question: Which type of urine sample is best for an accurate lab test to check for a bacterial infection?

options.A: Twenty-four hour collection
options.B: Clean-catch midstream sample
options.C: Random spot sample
options.D: First morning collection

explanation: The clean-catch method washes away skin bacteria from the outside, ensuring the sample shows what is actually happening in the bladder. [learn more](BMP110_U6_T6#BMP110_U6_T6_h2)

question: A doctor asks to measure the total protein a patient's kidneys release over a full day. What specimen should the midwife arrange?

options.A: A clean-catch midstream specimen
options.B: A timed twenty-four hour specimen
options.C: A first morning concentrated specimen
options.D: A random routine specimen

explanation: Measuring total daily output requires collecting all urine produced across a full twenty-four hour period to get an accurate total. [learn more](BMP110_U6_T6#BMP110_U6_T6_h2)

question: During a clean-catch procedure, why does the patient let the first bit of urine go into the toilet before collecting the sample?

options.A: To flush away germs near the urethral opening
options.B: To empty the bladder completely before testing
options.C: To ensure the patient has enough fluid intake
options.D: To prevent the collection cup from overflowing

explanation: Passing the first part of the stream clears out skin bacteria so they do not accidentally get into the collection cup. [learn more](BMP110_U6_T6#BMP110_U6_T6_h3)

question: When handling a sterile specimen container, what physical action must the midwife avoid?

options.A: Labeling the container with the patient's name
options.B: Touching the inner surface or rim of the container
options.C: Holding the outside surface of the cup
options.D: Placing a secure lid tightly over the top

explanation: Touching the inside or rim transfers bacteria from the hands into the cup, which ruins the sterile environment needed for accurate tests. [learn more](BMP110_U6_T6#BMP110_U6_T6_h3)

question: Where is the safest place to collect a urine sample from a patient who has an indwelling urinary catheter?

options.A: The open end of the drainage bag outlet
options.B: The bottom drainage bag tap
options.C: The junction connecting the tubing to the bag
options.D: The specialized needleless sampling port

explanation: The sampling port lets midwives collect fresh urine while keeping the system closed and protected from outside germs. [learn more](BMP110_U6_T6#BMP110_U6_T6_h4)

question: Why should urine samples for lab cultures never be taken from the main drainage bag?

options.A: The plastic bag material absorbs all the bacteria
options.B: The urine in the bag is always completely sterile
options.C: It is physically impossible to open the bag safely
options.D: Urine sits too long in the bag, allowing bacteria to multiply

explanation: Urine that sits in a collection bag grows bacteria over time, which can give a false impression of an infection. [learn more](BMP110_U6_T6#BMP110_U6_T6_h4)

question: What does a sweet, fruity smell in a urine sample commonly suggest?

options.A: High consumption of leafy vegetables
options.B: Severe bacterial infection
options.C: Presence of ketones from diabetes
options.D: Normal concentration after exercise

explanation: When the body breaks down fat for energy in uncontrolled diabetes, it produces ketones that give urine a sweet or fruity scent. [learn more](BMP110_U6_T6#BMP110_U6_T6_h5)

question: Which visual sign in a fresh urine sample should alert a midwife to a possible urinary tract infection?

options.A: Cloudiness with visible floating particles
options.B: A faint, slightly aromatic scent
options.C: A pale yellow and transparent appearance
options.D: A high volume of total output

explanation: Cloudy urine often contains pus, bacteria, and cellular debris which are signs of inflammation or infection in the urinary tract. [learn more](BMP110_U6_T6#BMP110_U6_T6_h5)

question: What is the main reason for gently tapping the edge of a dipped reagent strip against the side of the container?

options.A: To activate the chemical reagents more quickly
options.B: To remove extra urine and stop the chemical pads from running together
options.C: To sterilize the plastic strip before color matching
options.D: To cool down the temperature of the urine sample

explanation: Removing extra liquid stops the chemicals on neighboring pads from bleeding into each other, which keeps the color readings accurate. [learn more](BMP110_U6_T6#BMP110_U6_T6_h6)

question: Why is it important to follow the exact timing instructions when reading reagent strips?

options.A: Color reactions keep changing over time, leading to wrong results if read too late
options.B: The plastic strip will dissolve if left in the air too long
options.C: It prevents the patient from seeing their test results
options.D: The urine sample cools down and stops the chemical reaction completely

explanation: The chemical pads change color progressively over seconds and minutes, so reading them at the wrong time gives inaccurate results. [learn more](BMP110_U6_T6#BMP110_U6_T6_h6)

question: Where should the patient's identification label be placed when preparing a urine specimen for the lab?

options.A: Across the biohazard transport bag exterior
options.B: On the laboratory request form only
options.C: Directly on the body of the specimen container
options.D: Only on the removable plastic lid

explanation: Lids can easily get separated from cups in the lab, so putting the label directly on the container body prevents dangerous mix-ups. [learn more](BMP110_U6_T6#BMP110_U6_T6_h7)

question: What can happen if a urine sample is left sitting at room temperature for hours before reaching the lab?

options.A: The urine becomes completely sterile over time
options.B: Bacteria multiply and cells break down, changing the test results
options.C: The chemical composition of the urine freezes and solidifies
options.D: All protein disappears from the sample

explanation: Leaving urine out too long allows bacteria to grow and white blood cells to break down, which ruins the accuracy of the test. [learn more](BMP110_U6_T6#BMP110_U6_T6_h7)

question: What is the primary reason a clinician orders a stool specimen collection?

options.A: To assess the client's kidney function status
options.B: To monitor baseline blood pressure changes
options.C: To measure daily fluid intake and output
options.D: To investigate unexplained gastrointestinal symptoms

explanation: Stool tests are specifically targeted at finding the underlying cause of digestive issues like diarrhea, bleeding, or pain. [learn more](BMP110_U6_T7#BMP110_U6_T7_h1)

question: Why is screening for occult blood in stool clinically important for pregnant or postpartum women?

options.A: It prevents the onset of gestational diabetes mellitus
options.B: It helps detect hidden gastrointestinal bleeding from conditions like hemorrhoids
options.C: It measures the exact amount of dietary fiber absorbed in the colon
options.D: It confirms the exact gestational age of the fetus

explanation: Occult blood screening reveals microscopic bleeding in the digestive tract, which is common with pelvic pressure and hemorrhoids during pregnancy. [learn more](BMP110_U6_T7#BMP110_U6_T7_h1)

question: Why must the patient pass urine before collecting a stool sample?

options.A: To ensure the bladder is completely empty for an ultrasound
options.B: To speed up the transit time of the bowel movement
options.C: To collect a midstream urine sample at the same time
options.D: To prevent urine from contaminating the stool specimen

explanation: Urine mixes easily with feces during elimination and can contaminate the sample with bacteria and alter test results. [learn more](BMP110_U6_T7#BMP110_U6_T7_h2)

question: A patient scheduled for an occult blood test ate a heavy meal of red meat the night before. What is the most likely consequence?

options.A: A complete absence of stool output
options.B: A severely altered stool pH level
options.C: Immediate destruction of the sample container
options.D: A false-positive test result

explanation: Red meat contains animal hemoglobin that can react with chemical reagents, making the test look positive when no internal bleeding exists. [learn more](BMP110_U6_T7#BMP110_U6_T7_h2)

question: Which macroscopic characteristic suggests an upper gastrointestinal source of bleeding?

options.A: Frothy and pale yellow texture
options.B: Black and tarry consistency
options.C: Clay-colored and pale appearance
options.D: Bright red streaks on the surface

explanation: Blood from the upper digestive tract is digested along the way, turning dark and tarry (melena) by the time it is eliminated. [learn more](BMP110_U6_T7#BMP110_U6_T7_h3)

question: Why is collecting stool directly from the toilet bowl water discouraged?

options.A: Toilet water and chemicals contaminate the sample
options.B: Patients find the method too uncomfortable to perform
options.C: It makes macroscopic observation physically impossible
options.D: The sample will dry up too quickly in the bowl

explanation: Residual cleaning agents and toilet water alter the composition of the stool and introduce outside contaminants. [learn more](BMP110_U6_T7#BMP110_U6_T7_h3)

question: Why do stool samples for parasite examination sometimes need to be collected over several days?

options.A: Parasites are often shed intermittently in the stool
options.B: Single samples are instantly destroyed by body enzymes
options.C: The laboratory requires a large volume of waste daily
options.D: Patients cannot produce enough stool on the first attempt

explanation: Many intestinal parasites do not release eggs or cysts in every single bowel movement, making serial collection necessary. [learn more](BMP110_U6_T7#BMP110_U6_T7_h4)

question: What is the main reason stool samples for culture and sensitivity must reach the laboratory quickly?

options.A: To ensure the specimen container does not leak fluid
options.B: To prevent the sample from changing to a clay color
options.C: To allow the laboratory staff to check stool consistency
options.D: To stop normal bowel bacteria from overgrowing pathogens

explanation: If a stool sample sits too long at room temperature, normal bacteria multiply rapidly and can mask or crowd out harmful disease-causing organisms. [learn more](BMP110_U6_T7#BMP110_U6_T7_h4)

question: What is the most appropriate action after removing gloves used during stool collection?

options.A: Wipe hands with a dry paper towel
options.B: Apply lotion before touching equipment
options.C: Perform hand hygiene immediately
options.D: Rinse the gloves in warm water for reuse

explanation: Hand hygiene is mandatory after glove removal to eliminate any microorganisms that may have passed through microscopic glove defects. [learn more](BMP110_U6_T7#BMP110_U6_T7_h5)

question: Which of the following is NOT an appropriate infection control practice when handling stool specimens?

options.A: Decontaminating reusable commode equipment with disinfectants
options.B: Wearing clean disposable examination gloves during handling
options.C: Placing sealed specimen cups in leak-proof biohazard bags
options.D: Transporting unsealed containers in open trays

explanation: Containers must always be securely sealed and bagged to prevent spills and environmental exposure during transport. [learn more](BMP110_U6_T7#BMP110_U6_T7_h5)

question: When should the specimen container be labeled with the patient's details?

options.A: Before the patient attempts to produce any stool
options.B: At the end of the shift during handover rounds
options.C: Right at the bedside in the presence of the patient
options.D: After returning from the laboratory reception desk

explanation: Labeling specimens immediately at the bedside prevents dangerous mix-ups between different patient samples. [learn more](BMP110_U6_T7#BMP110_U6_T7_h6)

question: Why is it important to note recent antibiotic use on the laboratory request form?

options.A: It helps the laboratory calculate the exact weight of the stool
options.B: It proves the patient is paying for their diagnostic tests
options.C: Laboratories require drug receipts for insurance claims
options.D: Antibiotics can alter the growth of bacteria in stool cultures

explanation: Medications like antibiotics suppress normal or abnormal flora, which directly affects how the laboratory interprets culture results. [learn more](BMP110_U6_T7#BMP110_U6_T7_h6)

question: What is the main goal of first aid in an emergency?

options.A: To provide definitive surgical treatment at the scene
options.B: To document legal details before touching the patient
options.C: To preserve life and prevent the condition from worsening
options.D: To completely cure the patient of the underlying disease

explanation: First aid is immediate temporary care given to save life and stop things from getting worse until professional help arrives. [learn more](BMP110_U7_T1#BMP110_U7_T1_h1)

question: Why must a midwife check the safety of the environment before helping an injured person?

options.A: To make sure police officers are present to write a report
options.B: To prevent the midwife from becoming another casualty
options.C: To determine if the patient has health insurance coverage
options.D: To check if the hospital equipment is clean and sterile

explanation: Scene safety ensures that hazards do not harm the rescuer, maintaining a safe workforce to treat the injured. [learn more](BMP110_U7_T1#BMP110_U7_T1_h1)

question: What does the term 'Golden Hour' mean in emergency care?

options.A: The time required to complete a full nursing care plan
options.B: The first sixty minutes after a critical injury or medical crisis
options.C: The designated visiting hour for relatives in the maternity ward
options.D: The time it takes for a baby to take its first breath after birth

explanation: The golden hour is the critical time frame where rapid medical intervention gives the highest chance of survival. [learn more](BMP110_U7_T1#BMP110_U7_T1_h2)

question: A postpartum woman starts bleeding heavily right after delivery. Why is acting within the golden hour so important for her?

options.A: It prevents irreversible shock and organ failure from blood loss
options.B: It guarantees the patient will be discharged home by evening
options.C: It ensures the placenta is delivered completely within the hour
options.D: It stops the baby from crying too loudly in the labor room

explanation: Acting fast during severe bleeding stops the body from entering deep, irreversible shock, saving the patient's life. [learn more](BMP110_U7_T1#BMP110_U7_T1_h2)

question: What is the main purpose of triage in an emergency setting?

options.A: To decide which patients should be discharged immediately
options.B: To collect hospital fees before any treatment is started
options.C: To assign a private room to every incoming sick patient
options.D: To sort patients by urgency and treat the most critical first

explanation: Triage organizes patients so that the sickest people who might die without quick help get treated first. [learn more](BMP110_U7_T1#BMP110_U7_T1_h3)

question: Which incoming patient category should receive immediate attention during a busy emergency shift?

options.A: A woman actively seizing from eclampsia
options.B: A relative asking for a medical report form
options.C: A patient with a mild headache for three days
options.D: A woman needing routine antenatal booking

explanation: Active eclamptic seizures are immediately life-threatening and fall under the emergency category requiring instant care. [learn more](BMP110_U7_T1#BMP110_U7_T1_h3)

question: In the ABCDE primary survey framework, what does the letter 'C' stand for?

options.A: Coughing
options.B: Circulation
options.C: Contraction
options.D: Coma

explanation: In emergency assessment, C stands for circulation, checking pulses, bleeding, and perfusion. [learn more](BMP110_U7_T1#BMP110_U7_T1_h4)

question: Why is the primary survey performed using a strict ABCDE order?

options.A: To comply with paperwork rules set by hospital management
options.B: To test the memory skills of the attending junior nurse
options.C: To catch and treat the most life-threatening problems first
options.D: To make sure the patient falls asleep during the physical exam

explanation: The ABCDE sequence ensures airway, breathing, and circulation failures are fixed before moving to less urgent checks. [learn more](BMP110_U7_T1#BMP110_U7_T1_h4)

question: Which of the following is a classic sign of developing shock in an emergency patient?

options.A: Deep, relaxed breathing and quiet sleep
options.B: Warm, pink skin with a very slow pulse
options.C: Cold, clammy skin with a fast pulse
options.D: High alertness and a very low blood pressure

explanation: When the body goes into shock, blood is redirected to vital organs, making the skin cool and the heart beat faster. [learn more](BMP110_U7_T1#BMP110_U7_T1_h5)

question: Which condition is classified as a major obstetric emergency requiring instant action?

options.A: Itchy skin during the third trimester
options.B: Mild lower back pain at term
options.C: Postpartum haemorrhage
options.D: Normal painless Braxton Hicks contractions

explanation: Postpartum haemorrhage involves heavy bleeding after delivery that can quickly lead to maternal death if ignored. [learn more](BMP110_U7_T1#BMP110_U7_T1_h5)

question: What type of consent generally applies when an unconscious patient needs emergency life-saving care?

options.A: Delayed court consent
options.B: Implied consent
options.C: Family committee consent
options.D: Written informed consent

explanation: When a person is unconscious and facing a life-threatening situation, the law assumes they would want emergency treatment. [learn more](BMP110_U7_T1#BMP110_U7_T1_h6)

question: Why is accurate documentation of emergency care important for a midwife?

options.A: It provides a clear legal record of the treatments given
options.B: It replaces the need to talk to the doctor on duty
options.C: It stops relatives from asking questions about the illness
options.D: It guarantees the patient will pay all hospital bills promptly

explanation: Clear notes protect both the patient by ensuring continuity of care and the midwife by documenting actions taken. [learn more](BMP110_U7_T1#BMP110_U7_T1_h6)

question: What main feeling usually defines emotional trauma during a bad emergency?

options.A: Sudden physical numbness in the limbs
options.B: Total memory loss of the past year
options.C: Extreme physical hunger and fatigue
options.D: Intense helplessness and severe terror

explanation: Trauma can completely overwhelm a person's coping abilities, leading to deep feelings of helplessness and fear. [learn more](BMP110_U7_T10#BMP110_U7_T10_h1)

question: Why should healthcare workers care about a patient's emotions just as much as their physical cuts and bruises?

options.A: Physical injuries never cause any psychological changes
options.B: Patients will refuse physical treatment if they are smiling
options.C: Emotional shock always stops physical bleeding automatically
options.D: The mind suffers severe distress just like the physical body does

explanation: Recognizing emotional pain alongside physical injury helps provide complete, whole-person care during a crisis. [learn more](BMP110_U7_T10#BMP110_U7_T10_h1)

question: Which action shows a freeze response in someone who has just survived a disaster?

options.A: Demanding immediate financial compensation from officials
options.B: Climbing onto vehicles to direct oncoming traffic
options.C: Sitting completely unresponsive and staring blankly
options.D: Running frantically and screaming loudly at everyone

explanation: A freeze response makes a person temporarily shut down, leaving them unresponsive or staring into space. [learn more](BMP110_U7_T10#BMP110_U7_T10_h2)

question: How should we view sudden emotional stress reactions right after an emergency?

options.A: Normal, temporary responses to an abnormal event
options.B: Definitive proof of permanent mental illness
options.C: Deliberate attempts to avoid helping rescue workers
options.D: Signs of a pre-existing chronic brain disease

explanation: Strong emotional reactions are very normal human responses to frightening events and usually settle over time. [learn more](BMP110_U7_T10#BMP110_U7_T10_h2)

question: What is the main difference between Psychological First Aid (PFA) and formal psychotherapy?

options.A: PFA can only be performed by certified psychiatrists in a hospital
options.B: PFA is a supportive, humane response that does not require professional counseling skills
options.C: Psychotherapy is used exclusively at the scene of a road accident
options.D: Psychotherapy requires no training while PFA takes years to master

explanation: PFA is meant for everyday helpers to offer basic comfort and practical support without needing advanced therapy training. [learn more](BMP110_U7_T10#BMP110_U7_T10_h3)

question: A frightened survivor is sitting alone after a flood. Using PFA principles, what should you do first?

options.A: Insist that the survivor recount every detail of how the flood started
options.B: Leave the person completely alone until specialized psychiatrists arrive
options.C: Check the surroundings for safety, approach gently, and ask about immediate needs
options.D: Begin deep psychoanalysis to uncover childhood traumatic events

explanation: PFA always starts with making sure the area is safe, approaching with care, and finding out what the person needs right now. [learn more](BMP110_U7_T10#BMP110_U7_T10_h3)

question: Why is it important for healthcare workers to avoid giving false reassurances to worried families?

options.A: Families prefer receiving no information at all during a crisis
options.B: False statements automatically accelerate physical healing
options.C: Medical law strictly forbids speaking to relatives at the scene
options.D: Broken promises destroy trust when the true outcome becomes known

explanation: Being honest keeps trust strong between families and the medical team, even when the truth is difficult to share. [learn more](BMP110_U7_T10#BMP110_U7_T10_h4)

question: How should you talk to a frantic relative who is searching for an injured family member?

options.A: Shout loudly over the crowd to establish immediate dominance
options.B: Use complex medical terminology to prove professional expertise
options.C: Refuse to answer any questions until police clearance is given
options.D: Speak in a calm, steady tone and provide honest, clear updates

explanation: Staying calm and giving clear, truthful updates helps lower panic and builds trust in the care being given. [learn more](BMP110_U7_T10#BMP110_U7_T10_h4)

question: What is a good way to help a family experiencing sudden grief at an emergency scene?

options.A: Placing them in the center of the crowd so everyone can watch
options.B: Asking them to stand outside in the rain to cool their tempers
options.C: Moving them to a quiet, private space away from chaotic onlookers
options.D: Transporting them immediately to a distant police station

explanation: Giving a grieving family privacy protects their dignity and shields them from noisy crowds. [learn more](BMP110_U7_T10#BMP110_U7_T10_h5)

question: Why should we allow people to cry, weep, or shout openly during early grief?

options.A: They help speed up the physical healing of minor injuries
options.B: They indicate that the person requires immediate surgical intervention
options.C: They prove the family member has a pre-existing psychiatric disorder
options.D: They are natural human reactions to sudden, shocking loss

explanation: Expressing intense emotions openly is a healthy and natural way for people to process sudden shock and loss. [learn more](BMP110_U7_T10#BMP110_U7_T10_h5)

question: Which of these is NOT a reason to urgently refer someone for psychiatric help after an emergency?

options.A: Mild fatigue and quiet crying after a minor accident
options.B: Active suicidal ideation with a plan to self-harm
options.C: Uncontrollable violence directed at rescue workers
options.D: Extreme psychosis with hallucinations and paranoia

explanation: Quiet crying and tiredness are normal stress reactions, whereas violence, severe psychosis, and thoughts of self-harm need urgent psychiatric attention. [learn more](BMP110_U7_T10#BMP110_U7_T10_h6)

question: An accident survivor starts seeing things that are not there and threatens to attack anyone nearby. What is the best first step?

options.A: Ensure safety and initiate referral pathways for specialized psychiatric care
options.B: Scold the patient severely for disrupting the rescue operation
options.C: Ignore the behavior because it will disappear in five minutes
options.D: Leave the person alone in the dark until they calm down

explanation: Severe aggression and hallucinations require keeping the area safe and getting expert psychiatric help right away. [learn more](BMP110_U7_T10#BMP110_U7_T10_h6)

question: What is the main risk for healthcare workers who deal with trauma day after day without proper rest?

options.A: Compassion fatigue and burnout
options.B: Complete immunity to all future stress
options.C: Sudden improvement in night vision
options.D: Increased physical height and bone density

explanation: Seeing trauma repeatedly without taking time to rest emotionally can lead to exhaustion and emotional burnout. [learn more](BMP110_U7_T10#BMP110_U7_T10_h7)

question: Why is self-care considered a professional duty for midwives and nurses rather than a luxury?

options.A: It ensures they remain healthy and effective enough to care for future patients
options.B: Patients refuse treatment from nurses who look tired or weary
options.C: It guarantees that nurses will never experience physical illness again
options.D: Hospital management strictly punishes staff who drink water on duty

explanation: Nurses and midwives need to protect their own well-being to stay strong and provide safe, high-quality care throughout their careers. [learn more](BMP110_U7_T10#BMP110_U7_T10_h7)

question: What is the main goal of emergency casualty transport?

options.A: To complete the journey in the shortest possible time
options.B: To administer complex surgeries inside the moving vehicle
options.C: To transfer all administrative records before moving
options.D: To move the patient without causing further harm

explanation: The core objective of moving any injured patient is to ensure they reach definitive care safely without worsening their existing trauma or illness. [learn more](BMP110_U7_T11#BMP110_U7_T11_h1)

question: Why is moving a patient prematurely without preparation dangerous?

options.A: It can worsen the patient's existing condition during the journey
options.B: It always causes the transport vehicle to break down on the road
options.C: It increases the cost of fuel for the health facility
options.D: It prevents the receiving doctor from writing prescriptions

explanation: Unstable patients who are rushed without stabilization often deteriorate rapidly once movement and vibrations begin. [learn more](BMP110_U7_T11#BMP110_U7_T11_h1)

question: Which assessment framework is used to prioritize life-threatening conditions before transport?

options.A: ABCDE approach
options.B: FAST evaluation
options.C: Bishop score assessment
options.D: APGAR scoring system

explanation: The ABCDE method systematically checks airway, breathing, circulation, disability, and exposure to catch urgent problems first. [learn more](BMP110_U7_T11#BMP110_U7_T11_h2)

question: A bleeding postpartum mother is stabilized at a clinic. What must happen before she is placed in the ambulance?

options.A: Wait until her relatives arrive with full payment for fuel
options.B: Discharge her completely from the hospital registry books
options.C: Administer all routine postnatal immunizations
options.D: Ensure active hemorrhage is controlled and intravenous access is secured

explanation: Controlling bleeding and securing IV lines for fluid replacement are critical stabilization steps before moving a shocked patient. [learn more](BMP110_U7_T11#BMP110_U7_T11_h2)

question: What is the standard vehicle choice for inter-facility medical transfers?

options.A: Bicycle cart
options.B: Road ambulance
options.C: Commercial motorcycle
options.D: Local delivery van

explanation: Road ambulances are specifically designed to carry medical equipment and personnel alongside the patient. [learn more](BMP110_U7_T11#BMP110_U7_T11_h3)

question: Why should improvised transport methods be used with extreme caution?

options.A: They always travel faster than regular hospital vehicles
options.B: They require specialized pilot licenses to operate
options.C: They are too expensive for local community members
options.D: They lack proper support and can worsen spinal or bone injuries

explanation: Using makeshift stretchers or vehicles without suspension can aggravate trauma due to bumps and poor body alignment. [learn more](BMP110_U7_T11#BMP110_U7_T11_h3)

question: Which body parts should rescue workers bend when lifting a heavy stretcher?

options.A: Elbows
options.B: Waist
options.C: Knees
options.D: Neck

explanation: Bending at the knees and using leg muscles protects the rescuer's back from strain and injury. [learn more](BMP110_U7_T11#BMP110_U7_T11_h4)

question: Why are safety straps placed across a patient on a stretcher?

options.A: To make the stretcher lighter to carry
options.B: To restrict the patient from speaking during the trip
options.C: To prevent the patient from falling off during rough movement
options.D: To keep the patient's blood pressure artificially high

explanation: Straps hold the casualty securely in place when the vehicle navigates potholes, bumps, or sharp corners. [learn more](BMP110_U7_T11#BMP110_U7_T11_h4)

question: Which position is best for transporting an unconscious patient who is breathing normally?

options.A: Recovery position
options.B: Upright sitting position
options.C: Flat on the back
options.D: Knee-chest position

explanation: The side-lying recovery position keeps the airway open and stops vomit or saliva from entering the lungs. [learn more](BMP110_U7_T11#BMP110_U7_T11_h5)

question: How should a midwife position a pregnant woman in severe respiratory distress during ambulance transfer?

options.A: Trendelenburg position
options.B: Flat on her stomach
options.C: Standing upright
options.D: Semi-Fowler's position

explanation: Elevating the upper body slightly relieves pressure on the diaphragm and eases breathing difficulties. [learn more](BMP110_U7_T11#BMP110_U7_T11_h5)

question: What is a major challenge of monitoring patients inside a moving ambulance?

options.A: Road vibrations and noise can hide changes in condition
options.B: Patients sleep continuously and refuse to wake up
options.C: Medical equipment works faster while moving
options.D: The lighting is always too bright to see skin color

explanation: Background noise and motion make auscultation and visual checks harder, requiring extra vigilance from the attendant. [learn more](BMP110_U7_T11#BMP110_U7_T11_h6)

question: Why should the attending midwife keep talking to a conscious patient during transit?

options.A: To ensure the vehicle driver stays awake
options.B: To practice taking a detailed family history
options.C: To prevent the patient from falling asleep forever
options.D: To monitor their mental status and reduce anxiety

explanation: Conversation gives a quick reading of the patient's level of consciousness while easing their fear of the emergency trip. [learn more](BMP110_U7_T11#BMP110_U7_T11_h6)

question: What does the acronym ISBAR stand for in clinical handovers?

options.A: Injury, Speed, Breathing, Ambulance, Report
options.B: Immediate Signs, Blood pressure, Action, Result
options.C: Investigation, Summary, Bed assignment, Review
options.D: Introduction, Situation, Background, Assessment, Recommendation

explanation: ISBAR is a widely accepted communication tool that ensures all critical patient facts are transmitted clearly without confusion. [learn more](BMP110_U7_T11#BMP110_U7_T11_h7)

question: Why is a formal verbal and written handover necessary when arriving at a referral hospital?

options.A: It is only required for administrative billing purposes
options.B: It allows the transferring midwife to take over the receiving ward
options.C: It proves to the patient that the trip is finally over
options.D: It ensures seamless continuation of care and prevents loss of critical information

explanation: Clear handovers brief the new medical team on what has already been done and what urgent interventions are still needed. [learn more](BMP110_U7_T11#BMP110_U7_T11_h7)

question: What two chemical changes happen in the blood during asphyxia?

options.A: Low sugar and high lactic acid
options.B: High oxygen and low carbon dioxide
options.C: Low oxygen and high carbon dioxide
options.D: High iron and low potassium

explanation: Asphyxia stops normal breathing, causing oxygen to drop while waste carbon dioxide accumulates in the bloodstream. [learn more](BMP110_U7_T2#BMP110_U7_T2_h1)

question: Why does the brain suffer the most rapid damage during a severe lack of oxygen?

options.A: Cerebral blood vessels completely close during emergencies
options.B: Brain cells have a very high metabolic demand for oxygen
options.C: Brain tissue contains large amounts of stored glucose
options.D: The brain is the largest organ in the human body

explanation: The brain consumes a massive amount of the body's oxygen supply and cannot store it, making it extremely sensitive to sudden shortages. [learn more](BMP110_U7_T2#BMP110_U7_T2_h1)

question: Which of the following is an obstetric cause of asphyxia?

options.A: Carbon monoxide poisoning
options.B: Umbilical cord prolapse
options.C: Peanut aspiration
options.D: Smoke inhalation

explanation: Cord prolapse compresses the blood vessels supplying the fetus, cutting off oxygen delivery during labor. [learn more](BMP110_U7_T2#BMP110_U7_T2_h2)

question: How does severe eclampsia lead to an increased risk of asphyxia?

options.A: Liver damage stops red blood cells from carrying any oxygen
options.B: Kidney failure causes the lungs to fill instantly with blood
options.C: Seizures and reduced consciousness depress the respiratory drive
options.D: High blood pressure directly blocks the windpipe with fluid

explanation: Severe eclampsia causes convulsions and altered mental states that impair normal breathing patterns and protect reflexes. [learn more](BMP110_U7_T2#BMP110_U7_T2_h2)

question: What is the medical term for the bluish discoloration of the skin caused by low oxygen?

options.A: Pallor
options.B: Jaundice
options.C: Cyanosis
options.D: Erythema

explanation: Cyanosis appears when deoxygenated hemoglobin increases in the blood vessels near the skin surface. [learn more](BMP110_U7_T2#BMP110_U7_T2_h3)

question: What is a key sign of developing asphyxia in a newborn baby right after delivery?

options.A: A loud, angry cry with pink skin all over
options.B: Rapid kicking of both legs and heavy sweating
options.C: Limp muscle tone and a very slow heart rate
options.D: Active sucking movements on the hands

explanation: Deprived of oxygen, a newborn loses muscle tone and develops bradycardia, failing to transition smoothly to breathing air. [learn more](BMP110_U7_T2#BMP110_U7_T2_h3)

question: What does the letter 'B' stand for in the emergency ABCDE primary survey?

options.A: Bleeding
options.B: Brain function
options.C: Blood pressure
options.D: Breathing

explanation: The primary survey prioritizes Airway first, followed immediately by Breathing checks. [learn more](BMP110_U7_T2#BMP110_U7_T2_h4)

question: Why must a midwife check the airway before evaluating breathing in an emergency?

options.A: An obstructed airway makes checking or attempting breathing pointless until cleared
options.B: Breathing problems are rarely dangerous compared to airway issues
options.C: Airway checks take less than two seconds to complete
options.D: Hospital guidelines forbid checking the chest first

explanation: No amount of rescue breathing will work if a physical blockage prevents air from entering or leaving the lungs. [learn more](BMP110_U7_T2#BMP110_U7_T2_h4)

question: What is a major danger of performing a blind finger sweep to clear a blocked airway?

options.A: Spreading an infection to the rescuer's fingers
options.B: Scratching the patient's tongue and causing mild pain
options.C: Pushing the foreign object deeper into the throat
options.D: Breaking the patient's lower teeth

explanation: Blind finger sweeps can easily wedge a loose object further down the windpipe, worsening the obstruction. [learn more](BMP110_U7_T2#BMP110_U7_T2_h5)

question: A newborn baby is limp and not breathing after birth. What is the most important initial step after drying and warming the infant?

options.A: Open and clear the airway, then start ventilation if needed
options.B: Inject high doses of intravenous adrenaline immediately
options.C: Wait ten minutes to see if spontaneous crying starts
options.D: Give the baby a sweet oral glucose solution

explanation: Clearing the airway and providing positive pressure ventilation is the cornerstone of reviving a non-breathing newborn. [learn more](BMP110_U7_T2#BMP110_U7_T2_h5)

question: How often should vital signs be monitored immediately after a successful resuscitation?

options.A: Only when the doctor visits
options.B: Every fifteen minutes
options.C: Once a day
options.D: Once every six hours

explanation: Frequent checks every fifteen minutes help detect sudden relapses or complications early. [learn more](BMP110_U7_T2#BMP110_U7_T2_h6)

question: Why is continued observation necessary even after a patient recovers from an asphyxiic episode?

options.A: The body completely stops producing urine after oxygen lack
options.B: Secondary cellular damage and swelling can develop hours later
options.C: Blood pressure always remains dangerously high forever
options.D: Patients always catch a bacterial infection after choking

explanation: Reperfusion and ongoing inflammation can cause delayed organ injury long after normal breathing returns. [learn more](BMP110_U7_T2#BMP110_U7_T2_h6)

question: What color is blood coming directly from a damaged artery?

options.A: Pale pink
options.B: Bluish purple
options.C: Bright red
options.D: Dark maroon

explanation: Arterial blood is rich in oxygen, giving it a bright red color as it spurts under high pressure. [learn more](BMP110_U7_T3#BMP110_U7_T3_h1)

question: Why does arterial bleeding spurt instead of flowing in a steady stream?

options.A: Capillaries push extra fluid into the damaged vessel
options.B: Arteries are located closer to the surface of the skin
options.C: Blood is pumped directly by the heart's contractions
options.D: Air enters the open wound with every breath

explanation: High pressure surges from each heartbeat cause arterial blood to shoot out in pulses. [learn more](BMP110_U7_T3#BMP110_U7_T3_h1)

question: Which vital sign often changes first when a woman begins to bleed heavily?

options.A: Body temperature
options.B: Heart rate
options.C: Respiratory rate
options.D: Blood pressure

explanation: The heart beats faster to pump the remaining blood harder and maintain pressure when volume drops. [learn more](BMP110_U7_T3#BMP110_U7_T3_h2)

question: A postpartum woman has normal blood pressure but her skin is pale, cool, and she feels very anxious. What is the most likely reason?

options.A: She has a sudden infection causing her skin temperature to drop
options.B: She is experiencing a normal reaction to the cold delivery room
options.C: Her heart has completely stopped pumping blood to her lungs
options.D: Her body is compensating for blood loss by constricting blood vessels

explanation: Compensatory mechanisms keep blood pressure stable temporarily while shunting blood away from the skin, causing pallor and coolness. [learn more](BMP110_U7_T3#BMP110_U7_T3_h2)

question: What should you do if blood soaks completely through the first gauze pad you placed on a bleeding wound?

options.A: Wait for the bleeding to stop on its own
options.B: Take off all dressings and apply a tourniquet
options.C: Add another pad on top and keep pressing
options.D: Remove the soaked pad and wash the wound

explanation: Removing the first pad disturbs the clotting process and causes the bleeding to restart. [learn more](BMP110_U7_T3#BMP110_U7_T3_h3)

question: Why is firm hand pressure the preferred first-line treatment for external bleeding?

options.A: It mechanically compresses the broken vessel and helps blood clot
options.B: It cools down the tissue to prevent local swelling
options.C: It completely stops all blood flow to the entire body
options.D: It forces oxygen back into the open wound to heal tissue

explanation: Direct pressure physically flattens the torn vessel walls together so platelets can seal the gap. [learn more](BMP110_U7_T3#BMP110_U7_T3_h3)

question: Where should a tourniquet be placed on an injured limb?

options.A: Right on top of the open wound itself
options.B: Directly over the joint below the wound
options.C: As close to the fingers or toes as possible
options.D: Two to three inches above the wound

explanation: Placing the tourniquet slightly above the injury on single-bone sections of the limb compresses the main blood vessels effectively. [learn more](BMP110_U7_T3#BMP110_U7_T3_h4)

question: What is the primary danger of loosening a tourniquet after it has been tightened for a while?

options.A: It stops the heart from beating completely
options.B: It permanently stains the skin a dark purple color
options.C: It always causes the limb to heal crookedly
options.D: It can cause a sudden drop in blood pressure and release built-up toxins

explanation: Releasing trapped metabolic waste and sudden blood loss return into circulation can shock the cardiovascular system. [learn more](BMP110_U7_T3#BMP110_U7_T3_h4)

question: Which of the following is NOT a classic sign of hypovolemic shock?

options.A: High blood pressure
options.B: Confusion or restlessness
options.C: Rapid pulse
options.D: Pale and clammy skin

explanation: Blood pressure drops, not rises, when the body enters hypovolemic shock due to severe fluid loss. [learn more](BMP110_U7_T3#BMP110_U7_T3_h5)

question: Why is internal bleeding often more dangerous to diagnose than external bleeding?

options.A: Internal bleeding only affects elderly patients
options.B: Blood accumulates hidden inside the body without immediate visual confirmation
options.C: Blood inside body cavities does not cause changes in vital signs
options.D: Internal blood vessels do not have the ability to form clots

explanation: Without external pooling to see, caregivers must rely entirely on subtle vital sign changes and symptoms of shock. [learn more](BMP110_U7_T3#BMP110_U7_T3_h5)

question: Why is keeping a bleeding patient warm during transport so important?

options.A: Patients in shock always have a fever
options.B: Hypothermia worsens blood clotting problems
options.C: Warm blankets restore lost red blood cells
options.D: Heat stops the heart from beating too fast

explanation: Cold body temperatures interfere with the body's natural ability to form clots and stop bleeding. [learn more](BMP110_U7_T3#BMP110_U7_T3_h6)

question: You are handing over a hemorrhaging patient to an emergency team. What crucial detail about an applied tourniquet must you share?

options.A: The color of the fabric strap
options.B: The brand name of the device
options.C: The name of the nurse who bought it
options.D: The exact time it was applied

explanation: Receiving clinicians need to know how long the limb has had restricted blood flow to guide surgical decisions. [learn more](BMP110_U7_T3#BMP110_U7_T3_h6)

question: What is the primary underlying problem in all forms of shock?

options.A: Complete failure of the central nervous system
options.B: Inadequate tissue perfusion and cellular oxygenation
options.C: Severe elevation in systemic arterial blood pressure
options.D: Sudden and permanent cessation of heart sounds

explanation: Shock fundamentally represents a failure of the circulatory system to supply tissues with enough oxygen and nutrients for normal function. [learn more](BMP110_U7_T4#BMP110_U7_T4_h1)

question: Why can shock be dangerously deceptive in its early stages?

options.A: Patients usually fall into a deep coma before any physical signs appear
options.B: Urine output increases sharply to flush out accumulated toxins
options.C: Blood pressure remains artificially high due to widespread vasodilation
options.D: The body uses compensatory mechanisms to temporarily mask the drop in perfusion

explanation: Early compensatory responses like tachycardia and vasoconstriction keep vital signs stable at first, hiding the worsening internal crisis. [learn more](BMP110_U7_T4#BMP110_U7_T4_h1)

question: Which metabolic byproduct accumulates when cells are forced into anaerobic metabolism during shock?

options.A: Potassium chloride
options.B: Lactic acid
options.C: Sodium bicarbonate
options.D: Carbon monoxide
