explanation: Charting must happen right after giving the drug to maintain an accurate, truthful record of care. [learn more](BMP120_U2_T1#BMP120_U2_T1_h6)

question: What is the proper professional response if you accidentally make a medication error?

options.A: Keep quiet so nobody else finds out about the mistake
options.B: Blame the junior student nurse who was standing nearby
options.C: Report it immediately and take steps to protect the patient
options.D: Cross out the entry and pretend nothing happened at all

explanation: Immediate disclosure allows the medical team to monitor the patient and manage any adverse effects safely. [learn more](BMP120_U2_T1#BMP120_U2_T1_h6)

question: Where does a drug administered by the oral route primarily enter and absorb from?

options.A: The muscular tissue
options.B: The gastrointestinal tract
options.C: The venous blood supply
options.D: The respiratory system

explanation: Oral medications travel through the mouth into the stomach and intestines where absorption into the bloodstream takes place. [learn more](BMP120_U2_T2#BMP120_U2_T2_h1)

question: Why is patient cooperation particularly important when administering oral medications?

options.A: Clients must measure their own liquid doses
options.B: The client must willingly swallow the drug
options.C: It prevents the drug from tasting bitter
options.D: It speeds up the chemical breakdown in the liver

explanation: Unlike injections or intravenous drips, oral drugs rely entirely on the patient's physical ability and willingness to take the medication by mouth. [learn more](BMP120_U2_T2#BMP120_U2_T2_h1)

question: What is a major advantage of giving medications orally?

options.A: It never causes gastrointestinal upset
options.B: It works faster than intravenous injections
options.C: It bypasses the liver completely
options.D: It is convenient and economical for the client

explanation: Oral administration requires no sterile needles and is generally cheaper and easier for conscious clients to manage. [learn more](BMP120_U2_T2#BMP120_U2_T2_h2)

question: What does the first-pass effect mean for certain oral medications?

options.A: The kidneys eliminate the medication within the first hour
options.B: The drug dissolves instantly upon touching the tongue
options.C: The liver breaks down a portion of the drug before it reaches the rest of the body
options.D: The drug goes straight to the brain without stopping in the stomach

explanation: Blood draining from the stomach and intestines flows directly to the liver, where liver enzymes can metabolize and reduce the active drug concentration. [learn more](BMP120_U2_T2#BMP120_U2_T2_h2)

question: Why are some tablets manufactured with an enteric coating?

options.A: To allow the pill to be easily crushed into powder
options.B: To protect the stomach lining from irritation
options.C: To make the pill dissolve much faster
options.D: To give the tablet a sweet fruit flavor

explanation: Enteric-coated tablets resist stomach acid and only dissolve once they reach the less acidic environment of the small intestine. [learn more](BMP120_U2_T2#BMP120_U2_T2_h3)

question: What specific action must a midwife take right before pouring a liquid suspension?

options.A: Filter the liquid through sterile gauze
options.B: Warm the bottle in a basin of hot water
options.C: Shake the bottle well to mix settled particles
options.D: Dilute the mixture with equal parts honey

explanation: Liquid suspensions contain solid drug particles that settle at the bottom over time, so shaking ensures the client receives the correct dose. [learn more](BMP120_U2_T2#BMP120_U2_T2_h3)

question: Which of the following is NOT part of the standard five rights of medication administration?

options.A: Right time
options.B: Right client
options.C: Right dose
options.D: Right color

explanation: The standard five rights are right client, right drug, right dose, right route, and right time. Color is not one of them. [learn more](BMP120_U2_T2#BMP120_U2_T2_h4)

question: Why is checking a client's level of consciousness vital before giving an oral medication?

options.A: To verify that the client remembers their diagnosis
options.B: To determine if the liver is metabolizing drugs quickly
options.C: To make sure the client is ready to pay hospital bills
options.D: To ensure the client can safely swallow and avoid aspiration

explanation: A drowsy or semi-conscious client lacks the protective swallowing reflexes needed to keep oral medications out of the airway. [learn more](BMP120_U2_T2#BMP120_U2_T2_h4)

question: How should a midwife measure liquid medication in a medicine cup?

options.A: By measuring the weight using a clinical scale
options.B: By looking down into the top of the cup from above
options.C: At eye level against the base of the meniscus
options.D: While holding the cup up high near the ceiling lights

explanation: Reading the fluid level at eye level ensures accurate dosing by aligning your vision with the curve of the liquid surface. [learn more](BMP120_U2_T2#BMP120_U2_T2_h5)

question: Why must a midwife remain at the bedside until the client swallows the medication?

options.A: To record the vital signs immediately after the drug enters the stomach
options.B: To wash the medicine cup immediately while it is still wet
options.C: To engage the client in conversation and improve their mood
options.D: To confirm the medication was actually ingested rather than hidden or discarded

explanation: Staying ensures compliance and prevents clients from cheeking pills or hoarding them, which poses safety risks. [learn more](BMP120_U2_T2#BMP120_U2_T2_h5)

question: What tool is typically best for administering liquid oral medications to an infant?

options.A: An open glass tumbler
options.B: A standard metal teaspoon
options.C: A sharp hypodermic needle
options.D: An oral dosing syringe

explanation: Oral syringes allow precise measurement and slow delivery of small liquid volumes into an infant's mouth, reducing choking risks. [learn more](BMP120_U2_T2#BMP120_U2_T2_h6)

question: Why is polypharmacy a major concern for geriatric clients receiving oral medications?

options.A: Pharmacies charge too much money for elderly prescriptions
options.B: Taking many drugs together increases the risk of side effects and interactions
options.C: It causes solid pills to dissolve too quickly in the mouth
options.D: Older adults always forget to swallow their morning pills

explanation: Geriatric clients taking multiple medications concurrently face higher chances of adverse drug reactions due to slower physiological clearance. [learn more](BMP120_U2_T2#BMP120_U2_T2_h6)

question: What dangerous complication can happen if an oral medication enters a client's airway?

options.A: Rapid liver failure
options.B: High blood pressure
options.C: Severe skin rashes
options.D: Aspiration pneumonia

explanation: Inhaling foreign substances like pills or liquids into the respiratory tract introduces bacteria and irritants, causing lung infections. [learn more](BMP120_U2_T2#BMP120_U2_T2_h7)

question: What immediate action should a midwife take if a client begins coughing and choking while taking a pill?

options.A: Ignore the cough because it is a normal reaction
options.B: Stop administration immediately and help the client sit upright
options.C: Lie the client flat on their back to ease breathing
options.D: Force a glass of water down the throat to wash the pill away

explanation: Stopping prevents further entry into the airway, and an upright posture uses gravity to help clear the throat. [learn more](BMP120_U2_T2#BMP120_U2_T2_h7)

question: What does parenteral administration mean?

options.A: Giving medications by mouth to be digested
options.B: Administering drugs bypassing the gastrointestinal tract
options.C: Instilling liquid drops straight into the eye conjunctiva
options.D: Applying ointments directly onto intact skin surfaces

explanation: Parenteral routes involve injecting medications directly into body tissues or blood vessels, avoiding the digestive system completely for faster or safer delivery. [learn more](BMP120_U2_T3#BMP120_U2_T3_h1)

question: Why use an intravenous route instead of oral during an obstetric emergency?

options.A: Oral medications are completely prohibited in all maternity wards
options.B: Intravenous medications reach the bloodstream and act much faster
options.C: Digestive juices make oral drugs completely harmless to the body
options.D: Intravenous injections cause zero discomfort compared to swallowing pills

explanation: When every second counts, such as managing severe bleeding after birth, injecting drugs straight into a vein provides an immediate therapeutic effect. [learn more](BMP120_U2_T3#BMP120_U2_T3_h1)

question: What does a higher gauge number mean for a needle's size?

options.A: The needle is made of heavier metal
options.B: The needle is narrower in diameter
options.C: The needle is much longer in length
options.D: The needle has a wider bore opening

explanation: Needle gauge works inversely to size, meaning higher numbers represent thinner needles that create smaller puncture wounds. [learn more](BMP120_U2_T3#BMP120_U2_T3_h2)

question: Which needle is best for giving a thick, oily intramuscular medication?

options.A: A tiny tuberculin syringe with no detachable needle
options.B: A short needle with a very narrow lumen
options.C: A very long and extremely high gauge needle
options.D: A wider needle with a lower gauge number

explanation: Viscous solutions need a larger inner opening to flow smoothly through the syringe without clogging or requiring excessive plunger pressure. [learn more](BMP120_U2_T3#BMP120_U2_T3_h2)

question: What is the correct motion when cleaning an injection site with an alcohol swab?

options.A: Wiping back and forth horizontally across the skin
options.B: Starting from the center and moving outward in circles
options.C: Scrubbing vigorously in a random zig-zag pattern
options.D: Pressing the swab straight down without any movement

explanation: Circular motion from the center outward sweeps dirt and microbes away from the exact spot where the needle will enter. [learn more](BMP120_U2_T3#BMP120_U2_T3_h3)

question: Why let skin antiseptic dry completely before inserting a needle?

options.A: To ensure the skin surface becomes sticky for the tape
options.B: To keep the metal needle from bending upon impact
options.C: To prevent the alcohol from stinging the patient's skin
options.D: To allow the chemical time to kill microorganisms effectively

explanation: Antiseptics like alcohol need adequate contact time to destroy bacteria; injecting immediately before drying reduces their antimicrobial effectiveness. [learn more](BMP120_U2_T3#BMP120_U2_T3_h3)

question: Which intramuscular injection site is generally considered the safest for adults?

options.A: Deltoid muscle
options.B: Ventrogluteal muscle
options.C: Vastus lateralis muscle
options.D: Dorsogluteal muscle

explanation: The ventrogluteal site overlies the gluteus medius, away from major nerve pathways and large blood vessels, making it the preferred choice for deep IM injections. [learn more](BMP120_U2_T3#BMP120_U2_T3_h4)

question: What is the main purpose of the Z-track technique during an intramuscular injection?

options.A: To make the needle puncture feel completely painless for the patient
options.B: To speed up the absorption rate of water-soluble drugs
options.C: To prevent irritating medications from leaking into subcutaneous tissue
options.D: To eliminate the need for cleaning the skin with an alcohol swab

explanation: Displacing the skin before insertion creates a zigzag path that seals the drug deep within the muscle when the tissue returns to its normal position. [learn more](BMP120_U2_T3#BMP120_U2_T3_h4)

question: What term describes accidental leakage of intravenous fluid into tissues surrounding a vein?

options.A: Infiltration
options.B: Hemolysis
options.C: Embolism
options.D: Phlebitis

explanation: Infiltration happens when the IV cannula slips out of the vein or punctures through it, causing fluids to enter the interstitial spaces. [learn more](BMP120_U2_T3#BMP120_U2_T3_h5)

question: An IV infusion patient has pain, and the skin is pale, swollen, and cool. What is the immediate action?

options.A: Flush the intravenous line rapidly with sterile water to clear any blockages
options.B: Slow down the infusion rate and place a warm compress over the tubing
options.C: Reassure the patient that mild swelling is a normal part of receiving IV fluids
options.D: Stop the infusion immediately, remove the cannula, and site a new line elsewhere

explanation: These signs indicate infiltration, requiring immediate cessation of the infusion and removal of the device to prevent tissue injury. [learn more](BMP120_U2_T3#BMP120_U2_T3_h5)

question: Which medication is the primary emergency treatment for severe anaphylactic shock?

options.A: Oral antihistamine syrup
options.B: Adrenaline (epinephrine)
options.C: Intravenous paracetamol
options.D: Injectable magnesium sulfate

explanation: Adrenaline acts quickly to reverse life-threatening bronchospasm, mucosal edema, and low blood pressure during acute anaphylaxis. [learn more](BMP120_U2_T3#BMP120_U2_T3_h6)

question: What is the best way to prevent accidental injury to the sciatic nerve during a buttock injection?

options.A: Use a much shorter needle length regardless of the patient's body weight
options.B: Push the medication down the barrel of the syringe as fast as possible
options.C: Inject directly into the center of the visible gluteal muscle mass
options.D: Always select the ventrogluteal site instead of the dorsogluteal site

explanation: The ventrogluteal site is anatomically remote from the sciatic nerve and major blood vessels, making it much safer than traditional dorsogluteal landmarks. [learn more](BMP120_U2_T3#BMP120_U2_T3_h6)

question: What is the main benefit of using a topical medication?

options.A: It completely bypasses the need for patient consent.
options.B: It minimizes systemic side effects by acting locally.
options.C: It guarantees complete absorption into the bloodstream.
options.D: It works faster than intravenous injections every time.

explanation: Topical medications are applied right where they are needed. This keeps most of the drug out of the general circulation and prevents unwanted body-wide reactions. [learn more](BMP120_U2_T4#BMP120_U2_T4_h1)

question: Why is it helpful for a midwife to know that the skin is a selective barrier?

options.A: It proves that all skin creams work instantly.
options.B: It dictates how well a drug can penetrate the tissues.
options.C: It means medications can never cross the outer layer.
options.D: It shows that skin absorbs every chemical equally.

explanation: Because the skin is built to keep things out, the type of cream or ointment used determines how much medicine actually gets absorbed into the body. [learn more](BMP120_U2_T4#BMP120_U2_T4_h1)

question: Which layer of the skin is the main barrier against drug absorption?

options.A: Basal cell membrane
options.B: Dermal blood vessel
options.C: Stratum corneum
options.D: Subcutaneous layer

explanation: The stratum corneum is the outermost layer made of dead, protective cells. It blocks most foreign substances and chemicals from easily entering the body. [learn more](BMP120_U2_T4#BMP120_U2_T4_h2)

question: Why do medicines applied to the vagina absorb much faster than those put on regular skin?

options.A: Mucous membranes produce oils that dissolve all types of drug molecules.
options.B: Vaginal mucous membranes lack a tough stratum corneum and have rich blood supplies.
options.C: Vaginal tissues are always warmer than the external skin surface.
options.D: The skin on the body has a thicker layer of fat underneath it.

explanation: Without a tough outer layer, and with a rich network of blood vessels nearby, topical treatments can enter the bloodstream very quickly through mucous membranes. [learn more](BMP120_U2_T4#BMP120_U2_T4_h2)

question: Which topical preparation is a greasy, oil-based formula that helps trap moisture?

options.A: Pessary
options.B: Lotion
options.C: Gel
options.D: Ointment

explanation: Ointments have a high oil content. This creates a heavy barrier that stops moisture from escaping the skin surface. [learn more](BMP120_U2_T4#BMP120_U2_T4_h3)

question: What is the main difference between a cream and an ointment?

options.A: Creams are water-and-oil emulsions that wash off easily, whereas ointments are greasy and oil-based.
options.B: Creams are only used for systemic drug delivery through transdermal patches.
options.C: Creams contain alcohol to dry out weeping wounds while ointments add moisture.
options.D: Creams are solid blocks meant to melt at body temperature inside body cavities.

explanation: Creams mix water and oil together, meaning they wash off easily and do not leave a heavy, greasy feel like pure ointments do. [learn more](BMP120_U2_T4#BMP120_U2_T4_h3)

question: What is the main reason for putting barrier cream on a newborn's bottom?

options.A: To deliver antibiotics directly into the baby's bloodstream
options.B: To lower the infant's body temperature during a fever
options.C: To shield the skin from moisture and irritating stool enzymes
options.D: To cure systemic bacterial infections spreading from the gut

explanation: Barrier creams create a protective layer over the skin, keeping urine and stool from breaking down delicate baby skin. [learn more](BMP120_U2_T4#BMP120_U2_T4_h4)

question: Which of these is NOT a normal use for topical medications in midwifery?

options.A: Managing vaginal fungal infections
options.B: Treating severe maternal hypertension with a skin cream
options.C: Protecting infant skin from diaper rash
options.D: Relieving pain from perineal stitches

explanation: Severe high blood pressure needs systemic medications taken by mouth or through an IV, not a local skin cream. [learn more](BMP120_U2_T4#BMP120_U2_T4_h4)

question: Why should a midwife use a clean spatula instead of fingers to take ointment from a shared jar?

options.A: To prevent introducing bacteria into the container
options.B: To follow hospital rules on saving money on gloves
options.C: To make sure the exact dose is measured in grams
options.D: To prevent the ointment from absorbing into skin

explanation: Using bare or even gloved fingers directly in a jar can spread germs into the product, which might cause an infection later. [learn more](BMP120_U2_T4#BMP120_U2_T4_h5)

question: What is the correct way to apply a medicated cream to a mother's skin?

options.A: In a thin, even layer using gentle strokes following the direction of hair growth
options.B: By piling a thick mound over the lesion and covering it with heavy tape
options.C: By spraying it quickly from a distance without touching the patient
options.D: By rubbing it forcefully in circles until the skin turns bright red

explanation: Gentle strokes following hair growth prevent skin irritation and help spread the medication evenly without blocking hair follicles. [learn more](BMP120_U2_T4#BMP120_U2_T4_h5)

question: Why is it important to clean off old cream before applying a fresh dose?

options.A: To punish the patient for not cleaning themselves earlier in the day
options.B: To make the medication tube last longer between clinic visits
options.C: To prevent buildup and ensure proper contact between the new drug and clean skin
options.D: To ensure the hospital records match the pharmacy stock count

explanation: Old layers of cream can block fresh medicine from reaching the skin and can trap dirt or bacteria underneath. [learn more](BMP120_U2_T4#BMP120_U2_T4_h6)

question: Why is getting informed consent especially important when applying topical treatments in midwifery?

options.A: Topical drugs are always dangerous and require signed court documents.
options.B: Many applications involve sensitive areas like the perineum or breasts where privacy and dignity matter greatly.
options.C: Patients have the legal right to manufacture their own herbal creams at home.
options.D: Midwives cannot touch a patient's skin without a medical doctor present.

explanation: Treating intimate areas requires clear communication and respect for the woman's body to help her feel comfortable and maintain trust. [learn more](BMP120_U2_T4#BMP120_U2_T4_h6)

question: What is a common sign of a mild allergic reaction to a topical cream?

options.A: Complete numbness of the entire left arm and hand
options.B: Yellowing of the whites of the eyes within minutes
options.C: Sudden redness, itching, and burning at the application site
options.D: Immediate drop in the patient's blood pressure and pulse

explanation: A local skin reaction usually shows up right where the cream was applied, causing irritation, a rash, or itching. [learn more](BMP120_U2_T4#BMP120_U2_T4_h7)

question: What should a midwife do first if a mother develops a bad rash after using a prescribed cream?

options.A: Stop the medication, wash the area gently with water, and report the reaction.
options.B: Tell the mother to ignore it until her next scheduled clinic appointment next month.
options.C: Scrub the affected skin vigorously with harsh antiseptic soap and alcohol.
options.D: Apply a thicker layer of the same ointment to cover the new rash completely.

explanation: Washing the area stops further exposure to the drug, and reporting the reaction ensures the patient gets a safer alternative. [learn more](BMP120_U2_T4#BMP120_U2_T4_h7)

question: Which details must be written down when documenting a topical medication?

options.A: The cost of the tube of cream purchased from the pharmacy
options.B: Date, time, drug name, concentration, and application site
options.C: The brand of soap the patient used to bathe that morning
options.D: The personal phone number of the attending obstetrician

explanation: Good clinical records need precise details showing what drug was given, when it was applied, and exactly where it went on the body. [learn more](BMP120_U2_T4#BMP120_U2_T4_h8)

question: Why is checking back on a patient after applying a topical treatment important?

options.A: To confirm whether the treatment achieved its goal and check for adverse skin reactions
options.B: To ensure the patient throws away the empty tube of cream immediately
options.C: To collect data for a research paper on chemical manufacturing
options.D: To prove to hospital management that the midwife worked a full shift

explanation: Checking on the patient later lets the midwife see if the cream is helping or if it is causing any skin irritation that needs attention. [learn more](BMP120_U2_T4#BMP120_U2_T4_h8)

question: What is the primary advantage of delivering medication via inhalation?

options.A: It completely avoids the need for patient cooperation
options.B: It targets the airways directly and works very quickly
options.C: It only works for treating systemic blood infections
options.D: It ensures the drug stays in the lungs permanently

explanation: Inhalation delivers the drug straight to the respiratory tissues, providing a fast onset of action right where it is needed. [learn more](BMP120_U2_T5#BMP120_U2_T5_h1)

question: Why are smaller doses often effective when administered through the respiratory tract?

options.A: Inhaled drugs are heavier than swallowed pills
options.B: Stomach acids help break down the aerosol particles faster
options.C: The lungs have a massive surface area and rich blood supply
options.D: Liver metabolism increases the potency of mist particles

explanation: The extensive vascular network in the lungs allows for efficient absorption, meaning less medicine is wasted. [learn more](BMP120_U2_T5#BMP120_U2_T5_h1)

question: Which particle size range is considered ideal for reaching the lower airways?

options.A: 0.1 to 0.5 nanometers
options.B: 1 to 5 micrometers
options.C: 50 to 100 micrometers
options.D: 10 to 20 millimeters

explanation: Particles within this specific size range can bypass upper airway filters and settle deep within the bronchial tree. [learn more](BMP120_U2_T5#BMP120_U2_T5_h2)

question: What happens to very large medication particles during inhalation?

options.A: They get trapped in the mouth and throat
options.B: They evaporate before reaching the vocal cords
options.C: They pass straight through the alveoli into the blood
options.D: They dissolve instantly in the nasal passages

explanation: Heavy, oversized particles cannot make the sharp turns in the upper airway and deposit in the oropharynx instead. [learn more](BMP120_U2_T5#BMP120_U2_T5_h2)

question: Which inhalation device requires the patient's own forceful inhalation to pull powdered medicine out?

options.A: Standard Metered-Dose Inhaler
options.B: Compressor Nebulizer
options.C: Dry Powder Inhaler
options.D: Ultrasound Humidifier

explanation: A Dry Powder Inhaler depends on the strength of the user's inspiration to aerosolize and deliver the medication. [learn more](BMP120_U2_T5#BMP120_U2_T5_h3)

question: How does a standard nebulizer differ from a pressurized metered-dose inhaler?

options.A: A nebulizer requires no power source or gas supply
options.B: A metered-dose inhaler always requires an electric wall outlet
options.C: A metered-dose inhaler is only used for newborns in labor
options.D: A nebulizer turns liquid into a continuous mist using gas or air

explanation: Nebulizers run on compressed air or oxygen to aerosolize liquid medication over several minutes of normal tidal breathing. [learn more](BMP120_U2_T5#BMP120_U2_T5_h3)

question: How long should a patient typically hold their breath after inhaling a metered-dose medication?

options.A: No time is needed
options.B: Until they feel dizzy
options.C: Exactly 2 minutes
options.D: About 10 seconds

explanation: A ten-second breath-hold gives the microscopic drug particles enough time to settle onto the walls of the small airways. [learn more](BMP120_U2_T5#BMP120_U2_T5_h4)

question: A pregnant patient is about to use her metered-dose inhaler. What instruction should the midwife give her right before she presses the canister?

options.A: Take a short, shallow breath through your nose
options.B: Breathe out completely to empty your lungs
options.C: Blow air directly back into the inhaler opening
options.D: Hold a deep breath before putting the device in your mouth

explanation: Exhaling fully allows the patient to take a maximum slow, deep breath when the medication is released, improving lung penetration. [learn more](BMP120_U2_T5#BMP120_U2_T5_h4)

question: What common problem can happen if a patient forgets to rinse their mouth after using a steroid inhaler?

options.A: Permanent staining of the front teeth
options.B: Severe sudden swelling of the tongue
options.C: Complete loss of the sense of taste
options.D: Oral fungal infections like thrush

explanation: Residual steroid medication in the oral cavity encourages fungal growth, which rinsing and spitting out prevents. [learn more](BMP120_U2_T5#BMP120_U2_T5_h5)

question: Why is watching a patient demonstrate their inhaler technique more effective than just giving verbal instructions?

options.A: It replaces the need to check the expiry date on the canister
options.B: It proves the patient has memorized the drug manufacturer's name
options.C: It guarantees the patient will never need another prescription refill
options.D: It helps uncover hidden errors like poor hand-breath coordination

explanation: Patients often say they know how to use an inhaler while making mistakes that can be easily spotted during a physical demonstration. [learn more](BMP120_U2_T5#BMP120_U2_T5_h5)

question: Which of the following is NOT a typical side effect to watch for after a patient uses a fast-acting bronchodilator inhaler?

options.A: A slightly faster heart rate
options.B: Feeling jittery or restless
options.C: Severe drop in body temperature
options.D: Fine trembling of the hands

explanation: Bronchodilators stimulate the sympathetic nervous system, causing jitteriness and heart rate changes, but they do not cause hypothermia. [learn more](BMP120_U2_T5#BMP120_U2_T5_h6)

question: A midwife gives an asthma medication via inhaler to a pregnant woman. What is the most important clinical action to perform shortly after the procedure?

options.A: Assess the patient's breathing sounds and respiratory rate
options.B: Keep the patient lying completely flat on her back for an hour
options.C: Record the batch number of the inhaler in the main ledger
options.D: Restrict all oral fluids for the next four hours

explanation: Evaluating clinical parameters helps the midwife determine if the medication successfully opened the airways and eased breathing. [learn more](BMP120_U2_T5#BMP120_U2_T5_h6)

question: What is the primary reason for mastering medication mathematics in clinical practice?

options.A: To eliminate the need for physician consultations
options.B: To reduce the time spent charting in the ward
options.C: To increase the speed of medication distribution
options.D: To prevent severe patient harm from dosing errors

explanation: Accurate calculations ensure patients receive the exact therapeutic amount prescribed, avoiding toxicity or ineffective treatment. [learn more](BMP120_U2_T6#BMP120_U2_T6_h1)

question: Why does calculation anxiety commonly increase during emergency situations or night shifts?

options.A: Calculators stop working reliably in low lighting
options.B: Fatigue and high pressure can impair cognitive focus
options.C: Patients require higher doses of drugs after dark
options.D: Pharmacy stocks change rapidly during the night

explanation: Stressful environments and tiredness make it easier to miss small mathematical details like decimal placements. [learn more](BMP120_U2_T6#BMP120_U2_T6_h1)

question: How many milligrams are contained in one single gram?

options.A: 1,000 milligrams
options.B: 10,000 milligrams
options.C: 100 milligrams
options.D: 1 milligram

explanation: The metric prefix 'milli' denotes one-thousandth, meaning it takes 1,000 milligrams to make one full gram. [learn more](BMP120_U2_T6#BMP120_U2_T6_h2)

question: Convert a doctor's order of 0.5 grams into milligrams for proper administration.

options.A: 0.05 milligrams
options.B: 50 milligrams
options.C: 500 milligrams
options.D: 5,000 milligrams

explanation: To convert grams to milligrams, multiply by 1,000, which moves the decimal point three places to the right. [learn more](BMP120_U2_T6#BMP120_U2_T6_h2)

question: What must a nurse do first if the ordered dose and the stock dose are in different units?

options.A: Use a different formula entirely
options.B: Double the final calculated volume
options.C: Discard the medication immediately
options.D: Convert one value so both units match

explanation: Math formulas only work when the numerator and denominator share the exact same unit of measurement. [learn more](BMP120_U2_T6#BMP120_U2_T6_h3)

question: A patient needs 500 mg of ampicillin. The pharmacy supplies 250 mg per capsule. How many capsules should be given?

options.A: 0.5 capsules
options.B: 2 capsules
options.C: 4 capsules
options.D: 1 capsule

explanation: Using the formula: Desired (500) divided by Have (250) multiplied by Quantity (1) equals 2 capsules. [learn more](BMP120_U2_T6#BMP120_U2_T6_h3)

question: What does a 1% weight-in-volume (W/V) solution contain?

options.A: 1 gram of drug in 100 mL of solution
options.B: 1 milligram of drug in 100 mL of solution
options.C: 10 grams of drug in 1 mL of solution
options.D: 1 part of drug in 1,000 parts of solution

explanation: Percentage solutions are always based on parts per 100, where W/V refers to grams per 100 milliliters. [learn more](BMP120_U2_T6#BMP120_U2_T6_h4)

question: How many grams of active drug are present in 200 mL of a 2% solution?

options.A: 2 grams
options.B: 20 grams
options.C: 0.4 grams
options.D: 4 grams

explanation: A 2% solution means 2 grams are in every 100 mL. For 200 mL, multiply 2 grams by 2 to get 4 grams. [learn more](BMP120_U2_T6#BMP120_U2_T6_h4)

question: Why must children receive weight-based medication calculations instead of standard adult doses?

options.A: Pharmacies only stock liquid medications for infants
options.B: Their organ systems process and clear drugs differently
options.C: Their total body water percentage is lower than adults
options.D: They always absorb oral medications much faster

explanation: Immature liver metabolism and kidney function make children highly vulnerable to drug accumulation and toxicity. [learn more](BMP120_U2_T6#BMP120_U2_T6_h5)

question: An infant weighs 5 kg. The safe dose is 4 mg/kg. What is the total dose to administer?

options.A: 20 mg
options.B: 54 mg
options.D: 9 mg

explanation: Multiply the child's weight in kilograms (5) by the prescribed dose per kilogram (4) to get 20 mg. [learn more](BMP120_U2_T6#BMP120_U2_T6_h5)

question: What drop factor is typically associated with a standard microdrip infusion set?

options.A: 60 drops per milliliter
options.B: 10 drops per milliliter
options.C: 20 drops per milliliter
options.D: 15 drops per milliliter

explanation: Microdrip sets deliver 60 drops per milliliter, making it easy to calculate drops per minute as equal to milliliters per hour. [learn more](BMP120_U2_T6#BMP120_U2_T6_h6)

question: Infuse 1,000 mL of normal saline over 8 hours using a tubing drop factor of 15 gtt/mL. What is the flow rate?

options.A: 31 drops per minute
options.B: 208 drops per minute
options.C: 63 drops per minute
options.D: 125 drops per minute

explanation: Multiply 1,000 mL by 15 gtt/mL to get 15,000 drops. Divide by 480 total minutes (8 hours multiplied by 60) to equal 31.25, rounded to 31. [learn more](BMP120_U2_T6#BMP120_U2_T6_h6)

question: When should rounding occur during a multi-step medication math problem?

options.A: At the beginning before any formula is used
options.B: Whenever the decimal exceeds two digits
options.C: At the very end of the final calculation
options.D: During each intermediate division step

explanation: Rounding too early introduces cumulative mathematical errors that can significantly alter the final dose. [learn more](BMP120_U2_T6#BMP120_U2_T6_h7)

question: Which of the following practices is NOT recommended when verifying medication safety?

options.A: Performing a two-nurse independent double check
options.B: Checking stock labels carefully for correct units
options.C: Confirming the patient's weight in kilograms
options.D: Relying solely on memory without checking the formulary

explanation: Memory can fail under pressure; safe practice requires verifying doses against standard clinical reference texts. [learn more](BMP120_U2_T6#BMP120_U2_T6_h7)

question: What is the main difference between a drug side effect and an allergic reaction?

options.A: Allergies are predictable responses to the main goal of the medicine.
options.B: Side effects are predictable and mild, while allergies involve the immune system.
options.C: Side effects always require immediate emergency surgery.
options.D: Allergic reactions only happen when the drug dose is too high.

explanation: Side effects flow directly from how the drug naturally works in the body, whereas allergies happen because the immune system reacts abnormally to the substance. [learn more](BMP120_U2_T7#BMP120_U2_T7_h1)

question: Why might a patient experience an allergic reaction to a drug they have taken safely in the past?

options.A: The manufacturing company changed the color of the tablet coating.
options.B: The body can become sensitized during an earlier exposure and react later.
options.C: Past doses built up slowly in the fat tissue over several years.
options.D: Previous doses were too small to trigger any body response at all.

explanation: First-time exposure often primes the immune system without causing symptoms, making later doses trigger full allergic responses. [learn more](BMP120_U2_T7#BMP120_U2_T7_h1)

question: Which of the following is typically the very first sign of a developing drug allergy?

options.A: Sudden itching and skin redness
options.B: High fever with chills
options.C: Complete cardiac arrest
options.D: Severe kidney failure

explanation: Skin manifestations like itching, redness, or hives are usually the earliest physical clues that a drug is triggering an immune response. [learn more](BMP120_U2_T7#BMP120_U2_T7_h2)

question: How should a midwife interpret a mild skin rash appearing ten minutes after giving an intravenous antibiotic?

options.A: As an early warning sign that requires stopping the infusion immediately
options.B: As an unrelated skin infection caught from the hospital environment
options.C: As a normal side effect that will disappear if the patient drinks water
options.D: As a sign that the dose was too small and needs to be increased

explanation: Any new skin reaction shortly after an injection or infusion serves as an urgent warning that the drug must be halted to prevent severe anaphylaxis. [learn more](BMP120_U2_T7#BMP120_U2_T7_h2)

question: Which symptom points most clearly toward a life-threatening anaphylactic reaction?

options.A: A mild headache lasting for several hours
options.B: Dark discoloration of the urine
options.C: Swelling of the airway and severe difficulty breathing
options.D: Mild constipation after taking iron tablets

explanation: Airway compromise and breathing difficulty are hallmarks of anaphylaxis, making respiratory support the top priority in emergency management. [learn more](BMP120_U2_T7#BMP120_U2_T7_h3)

question: A postpartum woman develops sudden wheezing, low blood pressure, and widespread hives minutes after receiving an antibiotic injection. What is the most accurate clinical interpretation?

options.A: She is showing symptoms of normal postpartum hormonal shifts.
options.B: She is having a normal psychological reaction to the injection pain.
options.C: She is experiencing acute anaphylaxis affecting multiple body systems.
options.D: She has developed a mild side effect that requires simple reassurance.

explanation: The involvement of the skin, respiratory tract, and cardiovascular system simultaneously confirms a systemic anaphylactic shock event. [learn more](BMP120_U2_T7#BMP120_U2_T7_h3)

question: During which time frame do most severe, life-threatening drug reactions typically occur after an intravenous injection?

options.A: After one month of continuous use
options.B: Exactly one week after discharge
options.C: Within the first 30 minutes
options.D: Between 48 and 72 hours later

explanation: Severe acute reactions like anaphylaxis most commonly strike rapidly within the first half-hour following parenteral drug delivery. [learn more](BMP120_U2_T7#BMP120_U2_T7_h4)

question: Why must midwives pay special attention to patients with a history of asthma when administering new drugs?

options.A: They absorb oral medications much faster than other patients.
options.B: Their lungs are already filled with fluid from previous infections.
options.C: They cannot feel the early skin symptoms of an allergic rash.
options.D: They are at higher risk for severe respiratory compromise during a reaction.

explanation: Asthmatic patients have hyper-reactive airways, meaning any allergic bronchospasm can quickly become severe and life-threatening. [learn more](BMP120_U2_T7#BMP120_U2_T7_h4)

question: What is the single most important FIRST action when a patient shows signs of severe anaphylaxis during an IV drug infusion?

options.A: Ask the patient to walk around the room
options.B: Wait for the doctor to arrive before acting
options.C: Write an incident report in the ward register
options.D: Stop the drug infusion immediately

explanation: Stopping the entry of the offending drug is the absolute first priority to prevent any further allergen from entering the bloodstream. [learn more](BMP120_U2_T7#BMP120_U2_T7_h5)

question: A patient collapses with cold sweat and a thready pulse right after receiving an injection. Which medication should the midwife prepare immediately?

options.A: Adrenaline (epinephrine)
options.B: Oral rehydration salts
options.C: Paracetamol syrup
options.D: Routine multivitamin drops

explanation: Adrenaline is the frontline emergency drug that reverses bronchospasm and raises blood pressure during severe anaphylactic shock. [learn more](BMP120_U2_T7#BMP120_U2_T7_h5)

question: Which Nigerian agency is officially responsible for receiving reports of adverse drug reactions from healthcare workers?

options.A: NAFDAC
options.B: NMCN
options.C: NMA
options.D: FMOH

explanation: The National Agency for Food and Drug Administration and Control (NAFDAC) oversees drug safety and handles adverse reaction reporting in Nigeria. [learn more](BMP120_U2_T7#BMP120_U2_T7_h6)

question: Why is it crucial to document a drug allergy clearly on the front of a patient's case notes?

options.A: To alert all healthcare workers and prevent future administration of that drug
options.B: To prove that the midwife was present during the morning shift
options.C: To fulfill legal requirements without affecting patient clinical care
options.D: To ensure the hospital pharmacy can charge the correct medication fees

explanation: Prominent allergy documentation ensures that doctors, nurses, and midwives avoid prescribing or giving the same dangerous drug again. [learn more](BMP120_U2_T7#BMP120_U2_T7_h6)

question: What is another common name used for dangerous drugs in clinical practice?

options.A: Controlled substances
options.B: Over-the-counter remedies
options.C: Nutritional supplements
options.D: Broad-spectrum antibiotics

explanation: Dangerous drugs are legally and clinically called controlled substances because they are strictly regulated by law. [learn more](BMP120_U2_T8#BMP120_U2_T8_h1)

question: Why do dangerous drugs need much stricter management than normal antibiotics?

options.A: They expire much faster than other pharmaceutical items
options.B: They do not require a doctor's prescription to dispense
options.C: They are always manufactured as expensive liquid injections
options.D: They carry a high risk of abuse and dependence

explanation: Because these medications can cause physical and psychological addiction, they require much tighter control than standard drugs. [learn more](BMP120_U2_T8#BMP120_U2_T8_h1)

question: Which Nigerian agency primarily regulates dangerous drugs?

options.A: Standard Organisation of Nigeria
options.B: NAFDAC
options.C: Nigerian Medical Association
options.D: Federal Ministry of Education

explanation: NAFDAC is the federal body responsible for regulating food, drugs, and controlled substances in Nigeria. [learn more](BMP120_U2_T8#BMP120_U2_T8_h2)

question: What can happen to a midwife who handles controlled drugs improperly or illegally?

options.A: Mandatory attendance at a nursing seminar
options.B: A minor warning letter from the ward sister
options.C: A deduction of two weeks salary only
options.D: Loss of license and criminal prosecution

explanation: Breaking the laws that govern dangerous drugs is a serious offense that can cost a midwife their license and freedom. [learn more](BMP120_U2_T8#BMP120_U2_T8_h2)

question: What kind of container must be used to store dangerous drugs in the ward?

options.A: An unlocked plastic storage box on the desk
options.B: A glass shelf open to the main nursing station
options.C: An ordinary wooden drawer with a sliding latch
options.D: A double-locked steel cupboard fixed to the wall

explanation: Double-locked steel cupboards keep dangerous drugs secure and prevent theft or unauthorized access. [learn more](BMP120_U2_T8#BMP120_U2_T8_h3)

question: Who should keep the keys to the dangerous drug cupboard during a shift?

options.A: The midwife or nurse in charge of the shift
options.B: The hospital gateman on duty at the gate
options.C: The visiting relative of a patient
options.D: Any student nurse available in the ward

explanation: For safety and accountability, the midwife in charge of the shift keeps direct possession of the keys. [learn more](BMP120_U2_T8#BMP120_U2_T8_h3)

question: What book is used to keep a continuous written record of dangerous drugs in the ward?

options.A: The Controlled Drug Register
options.B: The outpatient attendance sheet
options.C: The general daily admission log
options.D: The hospital financial ledger

explanation: The Controlled Drug Register is used to track every single unit of a dangerous drug that enters or leaves the ward. [learn more](BMP120_U2_T8#BMP120_U2_T8_h4)

question: How should a mistake in the controlled drug register be corrected?

options.A: Tear out the entire page from the register book
options.B: Apply liquid correction fluid over the mistake
options.C: Use a pencil to overwrite the incorrect figures
options.D: Neatly rule through the error and countersign it

explanation: Transparent record-keeping means mistakes are never hidden; crossing out cleanly and signing keeps the record honest. [learn more](BMP120_U2_T8#BMP120_U2_T8_h4)

question: Why is a second nurse required when giving certain dangerous drugs?

options.A: To help physically hold the patient down during injection
options.B: To transport the empty ampoule back to the pharmacy
options.C: To write the doctor's prescription in the medical file
options.D: To witness and sign for any wasted portion of the drug

explanation: Having a witness ensures that any leftover medication is properly disposed of and accounted for. [learn more](BMP120_U2_T8#BMP120_U2_T8_h5)

question: What is the main danger of not recording a wasted drug portion immediately with a witness?

options.A: It immediately causes the remaining drug stock to expire
options.B: It prevents the patient from feeling pain relief
options.C: It creates suspicion of drug diversion and violates policy
options.D: It automatically invalidates the doctor's medical license

explanation: Leaving drug amounts unaccounted for without a witness signature can lead to accusations of theft. [learn more](BMP120_U2_T8#BMP120_U2_T8_h5)

question: What does a drug discrepancy mean in controlled substance management?

options.A: The medication expiration date is approaching next week
options.B: The storage cupboard key is missing from the hook
options.C: The doctor wrote the prescription using a black pen
options.D: The physical drug count does not match the register balance

explanation: A discrepancy happens when the actual number of drugs in the cupboard does not match what is written in the register. [learn more](BMP120_U2_T8#BMP120_U2_T8_h6)

question: What should you do immediately if you find a discrepancy in the dangerous drug register?

options.A: Alter the register balance to match the physical count
options.B: Ignore it if the missing quantity is very small
options.C: Report it immediately to management and start an audit
options.D: Wait until the end of the month to see if it resolves

explanation: Reporting missing drugs right away helps trace the issue, prevents cover-ups, and keeps patient care safe. [learn more](BMP120_U2_T8#BMP120_U2_T8_h6)

question: What is the simple definition of a wound?

options.A: A permanent scar left after surgery
options.B: A swelling caused by fluid accumulation under the skin
options.C: An infection deep inside the muscle tissue
options.D: A break in the integrity of the skin or mucous membranes

explanation: A wound is any disruption to the normal structure and function of the skin or mucous membranes. [learn more](BMP120_U3_T1#BMP120_U3_T1_h1)

question: Why is classifying wounds properly important in midwifery practice?

options.A: It entirely prevents scars from forming after a tear
options.B: It replaces the need for using sterile surgical instruments
options.C: It eliminates the need to document daily wound checks
options.D: It helps choose the right care plan and spot early infections

explanation: Classifying wounds guides clinical management, helps predict healing, and allows midwives to catch complications early. [learn more](BMP120_U3_T1#BMP120_U3_T1_h1)

question: Which wound type is a clean, straight cut made by a sharp instrument?

options.A: Abrasion
options.B: Puncture
options.C: Incision
options.D: Laceration

explanation: An incision is created by a sharp blade, resulting in neat, straight edges with minimal surrounding tissue damage. [learn more](BMP120_U3_T1#BMP120_U3_T1_h2)

question: A mother sustains a jagged, irregular tear in the perineum due to rapid baby delivery. What type of wound is this?

options.A: Incision
options.B: Laceration
options.C: Abrasion
options.D: Puncture

explanation: Tears caused by stretching or blunt force trauma result in jagged, irregular wound edges known as lacerations. [learn more](BMP120_U3_T1#BMP120_U3_T1_h2)

question: Which skin layer is affected in a superficial wound?

options.A: Muscle and bone layer
options.B: Epidermis only
options.C: Dermis only
options.D: Subcutaneous fat layer

explanation: Superficial wounds are restricted to the outermost layer of the skin, the epidermis. [learn more](BMP120_U3_T1#BMP120_U3_T1_h3)

question: What is a main feature of full-thickness wounds compared to superficial ones?

options.A: They only affect the top layer of skin and heal in a few hours
options.B: They heal entirely through simple surface cell regeneration
options.C: They extend into subcutaneous fat, muscle, or bone and require scarring to heal
options.D: They never require any form of cleaning or dressing

explanation: Full-thickness wounds involve deep tissue loss below the dermis, necessitating granulation and scar tissue formation for repair. [learn more](BMP120_U3_T1#BMP120_U3_T1_h3)

question: Which of the following describes a clean wound?

options.A: An uninfected surgical wound where sterile tracts are not entered
options.B: A surgical incision that is currently draining thick pus
options.C: An open accidental wound exposed to dirt and soil
options.D: A deep tear contaminated with bowel contents

explanation: Clean wounds are operative wounds with no inflammation and no entry into colonized tracts like the gastrointestinal or genital systems. [learn more](BMP120_U3_T1#BMP120_U3_T1_h4)

question: A postnatal mother has a perineal tear that shows pus, redness, and a bad odor. How is this wound classified?

options.A: Abrasion
options.B: Infected
options.C: Superficial
options.D: Clean

explanation: The presence of pus, foul odor, and localized inflammation indicates that active microbial infection has developed. [learn more](BMP120_U3_T1#BMP120_U3_T1_h4)

question: What is an episiotomy?

options.A: An infection of the uterine lining after delivery
options.B: A surgical incision of the perineum made during childbirth
options.C: A superficial skin scrape on the maternal abdomen
options.D: A natural tear involving the rectal mucosa

explanation: An episiotomy is a deliberate surgical cut made in the perineal tissues to facilitate the delivery of the baby. [learn more](BMP120_U3_T1#BMP120_U3_T1_h5)

question: Which degree of perineal tear extends deep enough to involve the rectal lining?

options.A: First-degree tear
options.B: Second-degree tear
options.C: Fourth-degree tear
options.D: Superficial abrasion

explanation: Fourth-degree perineal tears are severe injuries that extend completely through the anal sphincter and into the rectal mucosa. [learn more](BMP120_U3_T1#BMP120_U3_T1_h5)

question: What is a key reason for conducting regular wound checks?

options.A: To ensure the patient never feels any pain during healing
options.B: To catch early signs of complications and guide care decisions
options.C: To completely eliminate the need for wound dressings
options.D: To speed up natural skin color restoration after trauma

explanation: Regular assessment allows midwives to monitor healing progress and detect early complications like infection or wound breakdown. [learn more](BMP120_U3_T1#BMP120_U3_T1_h6)

question: Which of the following is NOT checked during a routine wound assessment?

options.A: The depth and size of the wound
options.B: The amount and type of wound drainage
options.C: The patient's shoe size
options.D: The condition of the surrounding skin

explanation: Shoe size has no relevance to wound assessment, whereas drainage, surrounding skin health, and wound dimensions are vital clinical indicators. [learn more](BMP120_U3_T1#BMP120_U3_T1_h6)

question: Which surgical wound is most commonly managed by midwives after childbirth?

options.A: Traumatic burn
options.B: Chronic leg ulcer
options.C: Episiotomy incision
options.D: Abdominal hernia

explanation: Midwives routinely manage surgical wounds resulting from childbirth, such as episiotomies and caesarean section scars. [learn more](BMP120_U3_T2#BMP120_U3_T2_h1)

question: Why is understanding normal tissue healing important for a midwife?

options.A: To prescribe strong antibiotics without a doctor
options.B: To quickly spot signs of abnormal healing and prevent infection
options.C: To calculate the exact date of the next pregnancy
options.D: To replace sterile surgical instruments during delivery

explanation: Knowing what normal healing looks like enables midwives to identify complications early and intervene appropriately. [learn more](BMP120_U3_T2#BMP120_U3_T2_h1)

question: Which phase of tissue repair happens immediately after the initial bleeding stops?

options.A: Maturation phase
options.B: Inflammatory phase
options.C: Proliferative phase
options.D: Remodeling phase

explanation: After bleeding is controlled through hemostasis, the inflammatory phase begins to clean the wound bed. [learn more](BMP120_U3_T2#BMP120_U3_T2_h2)

question: A postnatal woman is three weeks postpartum, and her perineal tear is building new tissue and contracting. Which phase of healing is this?

options.A: Inflammatory phase
options.B: Hemostasis phase
options.C: Lag phase
options.D: Proliferative phase

explanation: Building new tissue, granulation, and wound contraction are the key characteristics of the proliferative phase. [learn more](BMP120_U3_T2#BMP120_U3_T2_h2)

question: Which blood component sticks to injured vessel walls to form a temporary plug when bleeding starts?

options.A: Red blood cells
options.B: Plasma antibodies
options.C: Platelets
options.D: White blood cells

explanation: Platelets are the primary blood components that adhere to injured vessel walls to initiate clotting. [learn more](BMP120_U3_T2#BMP120_U3_T2_h3)

question: What is the main job of the fibrin mesh formed during the clotting stage?

options.A: To stabilize the platelet plug and seal damaged blood vessels
options.B: To destroy all bacteria entering through the skin
options.C: To prevent white blood cells from reaching the wound
options.D: To permanently replace damaged skin cells instantly

explanation: Fibrin creates a tight web that reinforces the fragile platelet plug to properly stop bleeding. [learn more](BMP120_U3_T2#BMP120_U3_T2_h3)

question: Which white blood cells arrive first at a wound site during the inflammatory phase?

options.A: Fibroblasts
options.B: Neutrophils
options.C: Osteocytes
options.D: Keratinocytes

explanation: Neutrophils are the initial wave of infection-fighting white blood cells to enter an injured area. [learn more](BMP120_U3_T2#BMP120_U3_T2_h4)

question: Why is mild inflammation a helpful and necessary part of tissue repair?

options.A: It completely eliminates the need for collagen production
options.B: It stops all blood circulation so the tissue can rest
options.C: It permanently closes the skin gap within a few minutes
options.D: It brings infection-fighting cells and growth factors to the area

explanation: Inflammation increases blood flow to deliver white blood cells and growth factors essential for clearing debris and starting repair. [learn more](BMP120_U3_T2#BMP120_U3_T2_h4)

question: What is the name of the cell that produces large amounts of collagen during tissue rebuilding?

options.A: Erythrocyte
options.B: Platelet
options.C: Macrophage
options.D: Fibroblast

explanation: Fibroblasts are the primary structural cells responsible for producing collagen and rebuilding the extracellular matrix. [learn more](BMP120_U3_T2#BMP120_U3_T2_h5)

question: What gives healthy healing wound tissue its pink, grainy appearance?

options.A: The formation of tiny new blood vessels
options.B: Bacteria fighting against white blood cells
options.C: A heavy layer of dead fat cells pushing upward
options.D: Old red blood cells trapped under the skin

explanation: Angiogenesis creates a dense network of fragile new capillaries that make granulation tissue look pink and pebbled. [learn more](BMP120_U3_T2#BMP120_U3_T2_h5)

question: Which type of collagen gradually replaces earlier tissue to increase scar strength during the remodeling phase?

options.A: Type I collagen
options.B: Type V collagen
options.C: Type IV collagen
options.D: Type X collagen

explanation: Type I collagen provides much greater tensile strength and replaces the weaker Type III laid down earlier. [learn more](BMP120_U3_T2#BMP120_U3_T2_h6)

question: What is the maximum percentage of original tissue strength a fully healed scar usually regains?

options.A: About 80 percent
options.B: Exactly 50 percent
options.C: Not more than 30 percent
options.D: Around 100 percent

explanation: Even after complete maturation and remodeling, scar tissue rarely regains full pre-injury strength, capping out around 80 percent. [learn more](BMP120_U3_T2#BMP120_U3_T2_h6)

question: Which medical condition is known for slowing down wound healing in postpartum mothers?

options.A: Physiological anemia
options.B: Diabetes mellitus
options.C: Postpartum amenorrhea
options.D: Gestational hypertension

explanation: High blood sugar and associated metabolic issues in diabetes impair immune response and collagen production. [learn more](BMP120_U3_T2#BMP120_U3_T2_h7)

question: Which nutrient is especially important for providing building blocks for collagen during tissue repair?

options.A: Simple sugars
options.B: Caffeine
options.C: Protein
options.D: Saturated fats

explanation: Protein supplies the necessary amino acids required for cellular proliferation and collagen synthesis. [learn more](BMP120_U3_T2#BMP120_U3_T2_h8)

question: Why should midwives encourage gentle care and hygiene for postnatal wounds instead of harsh scrubbing?

options.A: To speed up the remodeling phase to finish in 48 hours
options.B: To force skin edges to remain wide open for drainage
options.C: To completely stop all natural inflammation
options.D: To prevent infection while protecting delicate new tissue

explanation: Gentle care keeps the wound clean and guards fragile new blood vessels and cells from physical damage. [learn more](BMP120_U3_T2#BMP120_U3_T2_h8)

question: What is the primary goal of using aseptic technique during a midwifery procedure?

options.A: To remove all normal flora permanently from the mother's skin
options.B: To prevent germs from entering a sterile wound or body site
options.C: To cure an existing deep tissue infection without using drugs
options.D: To completely sterilize the air inside the delivery ward

explanation: Aseptic technique creates a barrier to stop harmful micro-organisms from getting into clean areas of the body. [learn more](BMP120_U3_T3#BMP120_U3_T3_h1)

question: What is the main difference between sterility and asepsis?

options.A: There is no practical difference between the two terms in daily clinical work
options.B: Sterility can be achieved with soap and water, while asepsis requires an autoclave
options.C: Asepsis applies only to surgical instruments, while sterility applies only to human skin
options.D: Sterility means zero living organisms, while asepsis means freedom from infectious material

explanation: Sterility is absolute, meaning completely free of all microbial life, whereas asepsis focuses on preventing the spread of infection-causing agents. [learn more](BMP120_U3_T3#BMP120_U3_T3_h1)

question: What action must you take immediately if you are unsure whether a sterile instrument has been contaminated?

options.A: Use it only if the patient has a strong immune system
options.B: Hold it over a flame for ten seconds before use
options.C: Treat it as contaminated and do not use it
options.D: Wipe it down quickly with methylated spirit

explanation: Safety rules state that any doubt about sterility means the item must be rejected to protect the patient. [learn more](BMP120_U3_T3#BMP120_U3_T3_h2)

question: Why is turning your back on an open sterile tray considered a breach of technique?

options.A: The sterile items will automatically cool down and attract moisture
options.B: Air currents from behind travel faster and carry heavy bacteria
options.C: You can no longer monitor it to ensure it remains uncontaminated
options.D: Hospital regulations require midwives to face instrument trays at all times

explanation: Unwatched sterile fields can easily be accidentally touched or contaminated by passing colleagues or movement without your knowledge. [learn more](BMP120_U3_T3#BMP120_U3_T3_h2)

question: Which part of an open sterile drape or field is safely considered non-sterile?

options.A: The exact center of the tray
options.B: The bottom layer resting on the table
options.C: The outer one-inch border
options.D: The metallic handles of the forceps

explanation: The edges are easily touched or compromised during handling, so the outer margin is always treated as contaminated. [learn more](BMP120_U3_T3#BMP120_U3_T3_h3)

question: Why must a midwife gather all dressing equipment before starting the procedure?

options.A: To comply with local laws regarding the storage of surgical cotton
options.B: To allow the cleaning solution enough time to evaporate in the air
options.C: To ensure the hospital inventory book balances at the end of the shift
options.D: To prevent leaving the patient unattended or breaking the sterile field later

explanation: Leaving a sterile setup to fetch forgotten items risks contamination and compromises patient safety. [learn more](BMP120_U3_T3#BMP120_U3_T3_h3)

question: In which direction should you wipe a surgical wound when cleaning it with antiseptic swabs?

options.A: From the center outward
options.B: From the bottom to the top
options.C: In a vigorous zig-zag motion
options.D: From the outer edges inward

explanation: Cleaning from the cleanest area (the wound center) to the dirtiest area (surrounding skin) prevents pushing skin bacteria into the healing tissue. [learn more](BMP120_U3_T3#BMP120_U3_T3_h4)

question: What is the correct action regarding gloves when transitioning from removing an old dressing to cleaning the wound?

options.A: Keep the same gloves on since you are working on the same patient
options.B: Wipe the dirty gloves thoroughly with spirit and continue working
options.C: Take off the gloves and perform the rest of the procedure barehanded
options.D: Remove dirty gloves, perform hand hygiene, and put on new gloves

explanation: Old dressings carry micro-organisms from the wound surface, requiring glove removal and hand hygiene to stop cross-contamination. [learn more](BMP120_U3_T3#BMP120_U3_T3_h4)

question: Where should you safely dispose of used surgical blades and suture needles after a dressing procedure?

options.A: In a puncture-resistant safety box
options.B: In an open plastic basin on the trolley
options.C: Wrapped inside the used cotton gauze
options.D: Inside the black domestic waste bin

explanation: Sharps must always go into a rigid safety box to prevent accidental needle-stick injuries to staff and cleaners. [learn more](BMP120_U3_T3#BMP120_U3_T3_h5)

question: Why is it dangerous to recap used needles after a medical procedure?

options.A: It makes the needle too blunt to use on the next patient
options.B: It exposes the sterile medication inside to room air
options.C: Hospital administrative policies forbid keeping needles in trays
options.D: It greatly increases the risk of accidental needle-stick injuries

explanation: Trying to guide a cap back onto a used needle often results in piercing your own finger, exposing you to blood-borne infections. [learn more](BMP120_U3_T3#BMP120_U3_T3_h5)

question: Why should you avoid pointing the tips of sterile forceps downward during a procedure?

options.A: The metal weight will cause the forceps to bend out of shape
options.B: Hospital protocol requires forceps to be held completely flat
options.C: It makes it difficult for your assistant to see the instrument
options.D: Contaminated liquids can flow down from your hands onto the sterile tips

explanation: Gravity pulls fluids downward; pointing tips down allows unsterile sweat or solution from your hands to contaminate the working end. [learn more](BMP120_U3_T3#BMP120_U3_T3_h6)

question: Which of the following actions is NOT safe when maintaining a sterile field?

options.A: Checking that the under-surface of the drape is dry
options.B: Keeping your hands positioned above your waist level
options.C: Reaching directly across an open sterile dressing pack
options.D: Discarding any instrument that touches an unsterile zone

explanation: Reaching across a sterile field risks shedding unnoticeable skin flakes or brushing the area with unsterile clothing. [learn more](BMP120_U3_T3#BMP120_U3_T3_h6)

question: Which of the following is a primary use of bandaging in postpartum midwifery care?

options.A: Lowering the patient's resting blood pressure
options.B: Securing dressings over caesarean section wounds
options.C: Replacing the need for routine perineal hygiene
options.D: Stimulating early postpartum breast milk production

explanation: Midwives frequently use bandages to hold protective dressings firmly in place over abdominal surgical incisions after a caesarean delivery. [learn more](BMP120_U3_T4#BMP120_U3_T4_h1)

question: Why does a properly applied bandage help promote the healing of a wound?

options.A: it delivers systemic antibiotics directly into the bloodstream.
options.B: It protects the tissue from contamination and absorbs drainage.
options.C: It permanently immobilizes the patient to prevent movement.
options.D: It completely stops all blood flow to the affected area.

explanation: Bandages act as a physical barrier against germs while managing excess fluid or exudate from the wound site. [learn more](BMP120_U3_T4#BMP120_U3_T4_h1)

question: What type of bandage is typically folded into a triangle and used as a sling?

options.A: Crepe bandage
options.B: Roller bandage
options.C: Triangular bandage
options.D: Tubular bandage

explanation: Triangular bandages are large cloth pieces specifically designed to be folded into slings for supporting limbs. [learn more](BMP120_U3_T4#BMP120_U3_T4_h2)

question: A pregnant patient arrives at the clinic with a severely sprained ankle requiring gentle compression and joint support. Which bandage should you select?

options.A: Crepe bandage
options.B: Tubular dressing
options.C: Plain gauze strip
options.D: Triangular sling

explanation: Crepe bandages stretch easily, making them perfect for wrapping joints like ankles to provide flexible compression and reduce swelling. [learn more](BMP120_U3_T4#BMP120_U3_T4_h2)

question: In which direction should a midwife generally wrap a limb when applying a roller bandage?

options.A: In any random direction that feels comfortable
options.B: Strictly from the middle outward to both ends
options.C: From the proximal end toward the distal end
options.D: From the distal end toward the proximal end

explanation: Working from distal to proximal helps push blood back toward the heart and prevents dangerous fluid buildup in the extremities. [learn more](BMP120_U3_T4#BMP120_U3_T4_h3)

question: Why is it important to leave a patient's fingers or toes exposed when bandaging a limb?

options.A: To prevent the bandage from absorbing natural body oils
options.B: To make it easier for the patient to remove the tape
options.C: To allow the midwife to monitor blood circulation easily
options.D: To keep the patient's hands or feet warm in the clinic

explanation: Exposing the tips of digits gives an immediate visual indicator of blood flow through color and temperature checks. [learn more](BMP120_U3_T4#BMP120_U3_T4_h3)

question: Why should a midwife never apply a bandage to a limb while it hangs unsupported in the air?

options.A: The bandage material will automatically tear from the weight.
options.B: Muscle tension can change the limb size, leading to incorrect pressure.
options.C: The patient will immediately experience severe bone fractures.
options.D: It violates standard hospital infection control protocols.

explanation: Unsuported limbs cause muscles to tense up, which distorts measurements and causes the bandage to become too tight or loose later. [learn more](BMP120_U3_T4#BMP120_U3_T4_h4)

question: What is the very first action a midwife should take before starting any bandaging procedure?

options.A: Cut the bandage into small, manageable pieces
options.B: Explain the procedure and gain the patient's consent
options.C: Elevate the patient's bed to the highest setting
options.D: Apply strong adhesive tape directly to the skin

explanation: Communication and consent build trust and ensure the patient understands what is about to happen during care. [learn more](BMP120_U3_T4#BMP120_U3_T4_h4)

question: Which bandaging turn is best suited for wrapping a joint like the knee or ankle?

options.A: Figure-eight turn
options.B: Simple circular turn
options.C: Basic spiral turn
options.D: Downward vertical turn

explanation: Figure-eight turns accommodate joint movement and curves securely without slipping off active joints. [learn more](BMP120_U3_T4#BMP120_U3_T4_h5)

question: When is a spiral reverse turn preferred over a standard spiral turn on a patient's limb?

options.A: When the patient is completely unconscious
options.B: When the limb changes diameter and tapers significantly
options.C: When the midwife wants to finish the procedure quickly
options.D: When the wound requires absolute airtight sealing

explanation: Tapering limbs cause normal spiral bandages to gap or slip, so reversing the turn helps the fabric lie flat against the skin contour. [learn more](BMP120_U3_T4#BMP120_U3_T4_h5)

question: What is a key indicator that a bandage has been applied too tightly and is cutting off blood flow?

options.A: A slight increase in the client's normal appetite
options.B: The bandage fabric changing its original color
options.C: The patient feeling warm and relaxed on the bed
options.D: Numbness, tingling, or coldness in the fingers or toes

explanation: Nerves and blood vessels suffer when compressed, leading to cold digits, tingling sensations, or numbness distal to the bandage. [learn more](BMP120_U3_T4#BMP120_U3_T4_h6)

question: A postpartum woman complains of sharp throbbing pain and swelling in her toes shortly after you bandage her lower leg. What should you do first?

options.A: Administer a strong prescription painkiller immediately
options.B: Promptly loosen or reapply the bandage to check circulation
options.C: Reassure her that this is a normal part of healing
options.D: Apply an extra layer of bandages to secure the area

explanation: Throbbing pain and swelling point to obstructed venous return, requiring immediate adjustment of the bandage tension. [learn more](BMP120_U3_T4#BMP120_U3_T4_h6)

question: What problem is caused by leaving wrinkles or folds in a bandage during application?

options.A: Rapid dissolution of the underlying wound dressing material
options.B: Localized pressure points that can cause skin breakdown and blisters
options.C: An immediate increase in systemic maternal blood pressure
options.D: Complete blockage of all lymphatic fluid throughout the body

explanation: Wrinkles press unevenly into the skin, causing friction and pressure sores if left uncorrected. [learn more](BMP120_U3_T4#BMP120_U3_T4_h7)

question: Which of the following is NOT a recognized complication of an improperly applied bandage?

options.A: Secondary infection due to a loose, slipping dressing
options.B: Skin breakdown caused by persistent wrinkles
options.C: Enhanced milk production in postpartum mothers
options.D: Tissue necrosis from restricted blood circulation

explanation: Bandaging limbs or wounds has no physiological connection to stimulating breast milk production. [learn more](BMP120_U3_T4#BMP120_U3_T4_h7)

question: Which suture type naturally breaks down inside the body over time?

options.A: Polypropylene sutures
options.B: Silk sutures
options.C: Nylon sutures
options.D: Absorbable sutures

explanation: Absorbable sutures are designed to be broken down and absorbed by body tissues, meaning they do not need to be pulled out manually. [learn more](BMP120_U3_T5#BMP120_U3_T5_h1)

question: Why are monofilament sutures often preferred to reduce the risk of infection?

options.A: They never require tying secure knots during a surgical repair
options.B: They stimulate rapid blood flow directly to the wound edges
options.C: They dissolve much faster than any other available material
options.D: They feature a single smooth strand that bacteria cannot easily hide in

explanation: A single smooth strand leaves fewer microscopic gaps or spaces where microorganisms can cling and multiply compared to braided threads. [learn more](BMP120_U3_T5#BMP120_U3_T5_h1)

question: How long should a newly sutured wound ideally be kept clean and dry after repair?

options.A: Exactly two full weeks
options.B: Until the patient finishes all meals
options.C: The first forty-eight hours
options.D: Only during the first six hours

explanation: Keeping the wound dry during the initial forty-eight hours helps prevent moisture from introducing bacteria into the fresh closure. [learn more](BMP120_U3_T5#BMP120_U3_T5_h2)

question: What is the best way for a mother to dry her perineal suture line after a gentle wash?

options.A: Rub the stitches hard with a rough towel
options.B: Pat the area gently with a clean, soft cloth
options.C: Use a hot hair dryer on the highest setting
options.D: Leave the area completely wet without touching

explanation: Patting avoids pulling or adding friction to the delicate healing tissue, whereas rubbing can break open the fresh wound edges. [learn more](BMP120_U3_T5#BMP120_U3_T5_h2)

question: Which of the following is NOT a classic sign of a healing wound becoming infected?

options.A: Spreading redness and warmth in the area
options.B: Pus or foul-smelling fluid draining out
options.C: A cool, pale skin surface around the stitches
options.D: Worsening pain several days after repair

explanation: Infection typically causes increased blood flow, warmth, and inflammation rather than a cool, pale appearance. [learn more](BMP120_U3_T5#BMP120_U3_T5_h3)

question: What does the term wound dehiscence mean in clinical practice?

options.A: The edges of the repaired wound pull apart prematurely
options.B: New skin grows too fast over the top of the thread
options.C: The suture material dissolves inside the body too early
options.D: A hard knot forms underneath the surface of the skin

explanation: Dehiscence happens when the closed wound edges separate or pop open before the underlying tissue has gained enough strength to hold itself together. [learn more](BMP120_U3_T5#BMP120_U3_T5_h3)

question: Why are facial sutures typically removed much sooner than sutures on the legs?

options.A: Facial thread material always dissolves on its own anyway
options.B: Leg muscles move constantly and push the threads out
options.C: Facial skin heals faster and experiences lower physical tension
options.D: Patients complain louder about stitches on their face

explanation: The face has a rich blood supply supporting rapid healing, and removing facial stitches early helps prevent permanent mark formation from the thread tracks. [learn more](BMP120_U3_T5#BMP120_U3_T5_h4)

question: A patient has non-absorbable stitches over her knee joint following a fall. When should the midwife plan to remove them?

options.A: Within forty-eight hours
options.B: In fourteen days or longer
options.C: On the third day
options.D: Between days four and five

explanation: Areas crossing joints endure constant stretching and movement, requiring extra time for the skin edges to gain enough strength before stitches come out. [learn more](BMP120_U3_T5#BMP120_U3_T5_h4)

question: Why must a midwife cut the suture thread close to the skin surface during removal?

options.A: To prevent pulling contaminated surface thread through the tissue track
options.B: To ensure the scissors remain sharp enough for the next procedure
options.C: To make sure the discarded thread stays long enough to reuse later
options.D: To prevent the patient from feeling any cold air on the wound

explanation: The exposed part of the thread collects bacteria from the air and skin surface; pulling that dirty section through the flesh can seed an infection. [learn more](BMP120_U3_T5#BMP120_U3_T5_h5)

question: What is the primary purpose of using dissecting forceps during suture removal?

options.A: To scrub away stubborn dried blood from the wound edges
options.B: To measure the exact length of the scar after healing
options.C: To gently lift the knot so the scissors can reach the thread
options.D: To inject local anesthetic pain medication into the skin

explanation: Forceps provide a secure grip to elevate the suture knot slightly above the skin level without causing trauma to surrounding tissue. [learn more](BMP120_U3_T5#BMP120_U3_T5_h5)

question: In which direction should a midwife pull the cut thread when sliding it out of the skin?

options.A: Away from the wound toward the outer healthy skin
options.B: Straight up toward the ceiling with a sharp jerk
options.C: Toward the wound line to keep the edges closed
options.D: In a fast circular motion to loosen stubborn knots

explanation: Pulling toward the wound pushes the edges together, preventing the newly sealed skin from tearing open again during extraction. [learn more](BMP120_U3_T5#BMP120_U3_T5_h6)

question: What critical final action must a midwife take after pulling out all the stitches?

options.A: Scrub the bare skin vigorously with a stiff brush
options.B: Prescribe a strong course of oral antibiotics
options.C: Apply tight pressure bandages for twenty-four hours
options.D: Count the removed pieces to ensure nothing is left behind

explanation: Counting ensures that no small fragment of suture material remains trapped inside the tissue, which would trigger an inflammatory foreign body reaction. [learn more](BMP120_U3_T5#BMP120_U3_T5_h6)

question: Why should a midwife advise a patient to protect a recently unsutured wound from tight clothing?

options.A: Pressure from clothing causes the skin to grow extra hair
options.B: Fabric dyes will permanently stain the healing scar dark blue
options.C: Friction from tight garments can irritate and break fragile new skin
options.D: Tight cloth stops blood from reaching the deep organs inside

explanation: Newly closed skin lacks the toughness of mature tissue and can easily chafe, blister, or tear when rubbed by tight fabrics. [learn more](BMP120_U3_T5#BMP120_U3_T5_h7)

question: What important warning should a midwife give a patient regarding her scar after suture removal?

options.A: The wound will completely disappear within forty-eight hours
options.B: She can safely scrub the area with soap immediately
options.C: The scar tissue takes several months to reach full strength
options.D: No further skin care or protection is ever needed
